#3416. Apple says it’s ‘only getting started’ updating macOS for touchscreens

Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display (pre-order here) includes a variety of software optimizations for touch input. But Apple says it’s “only getting started” making macOS more touch-friendly.

The new touchscreen-equipped MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR will ship with macOS 27.2, software that includes a variety of touch-centric optimizations that only impact PROLED XDR users.

Early feedback from hands-on testers, including our own Chance Miller, appears very positive.

Bloomberg’s Chris Welch reassuringly says that Apple is “taking a measured approach as it introduces touch capabilities.” This echoes comments from John Gruber, who says his concerns about touch “adversely affecting the Mac UI” have all been allayed.

But it sounds like Apple plans to roll out even more macOS optimizations for touch in the future.

An Apple employee answering press questions at Wednesday’s event said the company is only getting started optimizing macOS for a touch screen. I’d expect a slew of refinements to arrive alongside macOS 28 next year, much in the way the iPhone Duo’s user experience will inevitably evolve with iOS 28.

Overall, this isn’t necessarily reason for alarm if you’re worried about touch having a negative impact on macOS.

How about, spitballing here, a tablet device that takes advantage of MacOS’s new found touch capabilities? 🙄

Even though Apple has prepared an initial set of macOS changes to support touch input, it’s only natural for the company to continue refining the touch experience in response to early adopter feedback and usage patterns. My assumption is that the same “measured approach” we’re seeing right now will continue guiding these future macOS enhancements.

You can pre-order MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR on Amazon for day-one delivery.

Terrance Banks -- the man accused of killing 15 dogs in Florida -- seemed ready to go to jail when cops arrived the day he was arrested ... spinning around and putting his hands behind his back with no direction from officers.

Body cam footage from the tragic day shows officers walking up to Banks ... asking him for help identifying and corralling several dogs who are loose in the neighborhood -- telling him he's the only one who can help them do so.

Terrance, however, seems distraught ... repeating several times that it's simply over ... and moving to put his hands behind his back.

The cops tell him at first they don't want to arrest him ... they just want to know what happened -- and they want him to jump into action.

Ultimately, he is cuffed ... but the officers are clearly showing concern for him during their conversation.

15 of the dogs were later reported dead ... while two needed round-the-clock care after the shocking blaze.

Banks was arrested for second-degree arson and 11 counts of aggravated animal cruelty.

#3414. 10 Shows Like 'The Diplomat' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following its recently concluded fourth season, Netflix's political thriller The Diplomat has been renewed for a fifth season, and even better, it's the rare streaming show that seems to keep to a fairly regular schedule, meaning there's likely to be more of the Keri Russell-led espionage drama coming by late next year. If you're looking for something with the same political thriller vibes to watch in the meantime, here are 10 other series to stream now.

Diplomat creator Debora Cahn got her start on The West Wing, but honed her political-espionage craft on this show, for which she served as writer and, later, executive producer. The series begins with CIA case officer Carrie Mathison (Claire Danes) coming to suspect that decorated Marine Corps scout sniper Nicholas Brody (Damian Lewis), recently rescued from an al-Qaeda compound, has been turned and is planning a terrorist attack on the United States. As she has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, her superiors don't give Mathison's suspicions much credence, kicking off a cat-and-mouse/is-he-or-isn't he? game between the two. As the show progresses, Carrie moves up the ranks until she's working directly for the president. Both leads won Emmys for their performances, and the series took the Outstanding Drama prize in its first year. Stream Homeland on Hulu and Netflix.

Focusing largely on the seedier side of international espionage, Slow Horses, based on the novels by Mick Herron, shares with The Diplomat a dry sense of humor about the consequences of institutional and human failures. With nods to the great spy dramas of John le Carré, Slow Horses updates the setting without losing either the thrills or the style of a time-honored genre. The “Slow Horses” of the title are a group of has-been MI5 agents—they’ve all made messes of significant jobs, but are still seen as having some use, if only in dull administrative tasks. Naturally, the members of the group (led by Gary Oldman's endlessly flatulent Jackson Lamb) find themselves in deeper waters than anyone thought them capable of navigating. Kristin Scott Thomas is the spymaster, navigating political pressures, misogyny, and her own unrepentant ambition in trying to do her job. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings (dream job, honestly), until the night it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed; unbeknownst to her, they were also government operatives, and rescuing Rose sees Peter delving deep inside a web of conspiracy and corruption that plays out over three seasons, with a fourth and final on the way. While a bit more action-heavy than The Diplomat, it still plays in that realm of government secrets and conspiracies. Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There was a moment, around the turn of the millennium, when The West Wing seemed like a heightened but not entirely implausible picture of politics in action; its ripped-from-the-headlines style gave it an edge that allowed us to imagine smart, thoughtful people getting jobs in government, trying to do the more-or-less right thing despite systemic and personal flaws (it's also where The Diplomat's creator Debora Cahn started her TV writing career). The show's world can be a little frustrating when contrasted against our more explicitly appalling actual one, but it's a thoroughly pleasing fantasy nonetheless, with President Matin Sheen leading a White House staff through various diplomatic, military, and political crises. Stream The West Wing on Netflix and HBO Max.

Sidse Babett Knudsen stars as Birgitte Nyborg in this popular import. She's a minor Danish politician who watches other politicians fall to scandal and incompetence as she rapidly and unexpectedly ascends to the job of prime minister. The espionage and action are entirely incidental (but not nonexistent) here, as the show deals instead with the moral and political compromises that are seemingly intrinsic to statecraft. There's been talk of an American remake for years now, but you should just watch the original. Stream Borgen on Netflix.

Shonda Rhimes was already a powerhouse producer and screenwriter with several successful seasons of Grey's Anatomy under her belt when Scandal debuted, but its blend of political thrills and sexy, soapy drama truly solidified her brand—and her spot atop the modern TV landscape. Kerry Washington stars as Olivia Pope, head of the D.C.-based crisis management firm Olivia Pope & Associates (OPA), who is the person to call when you've got a PR disaster to fix. If you want to get a sense of the stakes involved, consider that Tony Goldwyn costars as Fitzgerald Grant III, who is both the president of the United States. and also Olivia's lover. Stream Scandal on Hulu and Netflix.

Téa Leoni plays Elizabeth McCord, a former CIA analyst who gave up that hectic life to become a political science professor. That's all going great until the Secretary of State dies under mysterious circumstances and she's called up by her old CIA boss, who's now the president, to take over the job. With her outsider's perspective and resistance to political considerations, she's surprisingly good at the gig, navigating foreign and domestic crises while also trying to figure out who the hell killed her predecessor, and whether they're coming for her, too. Stream Madam Secretary on The Roku Channel.

You could absolutely watch the original American take on this show, which stars Kiefer Sutherland—they have essentially the same premise—but this South Korean remake earns a few extra points by only running for a compact 16 episodes, making it far leaner and meaner. Education Minister Park Mu-jin (Ji Jin-hee) is fired from his job one day before an attack occurs amid an announcement of peace talks with the North, wiping out the entire presidential line of succession. His dismissal having not yet been finalized, the largely unambitious Minister Park is forced into the job, even as questions linger over the attack that put him in the role. Stream Designated Survivor: 60 Days on Netflix.

It's a different time and setting, but all the Keri Russell spy action you could want as a Diplomat fan. Set during the Cold War 1980s and created by former CIA officer Joe Weisberg, The Americans follows Soviet KGB intelligence agents Elizabeth (Russell) and Philip Jennings (the ever-reliable Matthew Rhys), living undercover lives posing as an American couple in the DC metro area—and raising their American-born children. The critically acclaimed show makes much of its period setting and a central conflict that places two spies in the heart of suburban America, even as they're tasked with undermining the Reagan-era government under which their children are growing up. Stream The Americans on Hulu.

A power struggle for leadership of an entire country is at the heart of this juicy political thriller. Prime Minister Park Dong-ho comes to believe that the president has been corrupted by powerful, wealthy individuals and companies (something that could only happen in South Korea, obviously). Deputy Prime Minister Jeong Su-jin sees the problem, too, but she's not so sure about his solution: He wants to have the president assassinated. But how much better is he than the man he would be replacing? And how pure are her motives in potentially putting herself in line for the top job? Stream The Whirlwind on Netflix.

#3413. iOS 27.2 adds new video feature that’s perfect for iPhone Duo

iOS 27.2 launched this week with many new features, including an upgrade for the Apple TV app that’s especially perfect for iPhone Duo: Multiview.

Apple TV’s growing lineup of sports content includes Formula 1, Major League Soccer (MLS), and Major League Baseball (MLB).

And a new video feature in iOS 27.2—Multiview—makes me hope the streamer adds even more sports soon.

Multiview lets iPhone users watch up to four live sports streams simultaneously. It’s available for all sports events included in an Apple TV subscription. Previously, Multiview was only available on Apple TV, iPad, and Vision Pro.

Activating Multiview is easy. Once you start watching a sports event you’ll see a new ‘Multiview’ button at the bottom of the Apple TV player.

Each sport’s implementation will differ a bit, but with F1 you can choose from a preset team Multiview or build your own custom setup that includes driver-view cameras, course maps, and more.

I gave it a try on my iPhone 18 Pro, where I assumed the smaller display would be a limiting factor on the number of streams. Fortunately that wasn’t the case, as I was able to set up four F1 streams from the Austin Grand Prix and could see all four on-screen at once.

Where I imagine this will prove especially nice is on iPhone Duo. Though it’s great that smaller iPhones support Multiview, the ability to stream four video feeds at once on the Duo’s large display sounds fantastic.

Do you plan to give Multiview a try on your iPhone? Let us know in the comments.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month, or you can get it discounted through the Apple One bundle.

#3412. Ex-Ohio State Professor Kills Wife, Tries to Stab Dog After Nude Photo Blackmail Threats

A former Ohio State University professor has been sentenced to life in prison after admitting he stabbed his wife to death in a shocking murder he claims was triggered by an online sextortion scheme.

77-year-old James Hill, a retired Ohio State music professor, confessed to killing his wife, attempting to stab his dog, and then plunging a knife into his own chest after a woman he met online allegedly threatened to release his nude photos unless he paid her $15,000 in Apple gift cards.

According to court documents, Hill told investigators he believed the only way out of the situation was to kill his entire family.

On November 9, 2025, Hill says he received a threatening message from a woman he'd been communicating with online. He'd previously sent her nude photos. The woman allegedly demanded $15,000 in Apple gift cards, threatening to expose his explicit photos if he didn't pay up.

Hill claimed he felt trapped and saw no other way out.

He told investigators he initially went looking for his gun, but couldn't find it, claiming his 64-year-old wife, Mary, had hidden the firearm years earlier. So, instead, he grabbed a knife.

Hill told local authorities that Mary was sitting at her computer in the couple's den when he approached her from behind and began rubbing her shoulders.

She reportedly told him it felt "good" ... but what happened next was horrifying.

Hill says he pulled a knife from his belt and stabbed his wife once in the chest. He told investigators Mary looked directly at him as he stabbed her, and he apologized while holding her as she died.

He told authorities he then walked into the living room and attempted to stab the couple's dog. According to court documents, the dog was struck but managed to escape before Hill could do anything more.

And before calling for help, Hill allegedly logged onto his computer and deleted several photos and documents.

Around 2:30 PM that afternoon, Hill finally called 911, telling the dispatcher, "We need police and an ambulance."

But when the dispatcher asked what was happening, the call abruptly disconnected.

Hill then unlocked his front door, sat down on his couch, and stabbed himself in the chest.

According to WBNS, he remained on the couch until officers arrived just four minutes later.

Court documents obtained by TMZ show Hill initially pleaded not guilty to his wife's murder. However, on October 28, 2026, he withdrew that plea and pleaded guilty to felony murder and cruelty to a companion animal.

Hill was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole after 15 years.

That means the 77-year-old could potentially be eligible for parole in his early 90s.

#3409. Apple VP talks new iPad mini: OLED without ProMotion, Acoustic Display, more

Apple unveiled its “biggest update ever” for the iPad mini this week, introducing a thinner, lighter design and an OLED display.

In a pair of interviews, Dave Pakula, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering, discussed the new iPad mini’s design, display, and more.

While the new iPad mini features an OLED display, it doesn’t support ProMotion. Instead, it’s limited to a 60Hz refresh rate. Here’s what Pakula had to say about that decision in an interview with Chris Lawley:

Display experience is about more than just a single spec. One of the things that’s really cool about OLED is it actually has this really fast pixel response time. So it’s more than an order of magnitude faster than the pixel response time for an LCD display.

What that does is it makes everything really smooth. Motion blur is significantly reduced compared to LCD. When you pair that with the other things, the contrast, the brightness, and the color, this is just a killer display.

In addition to being lighter and thinner, the new iPad mini is also IP67-rated for water and dust resistance, a first for an iPad. One key enabler is a new Acoustic Display. Pakula explains how that technology works:

One of the cool things we realized as we started experimenting was that the unique size and form factor of this display actually had a resonant frequency that’s in the audible range.

I think more importantly, it’s in the range of like a traditional woofer that you’d have in a speaker. What we did was we built these custom drivers that actually energize the display and emit sound directly through the enclosure, but that only really works for the mid and low frequencies.

For the higher frequencies, we actually designed these little custom tweeters. There’s one on each end of the product, and they’re actually ported out through these hidden ports between the glass and the aluminum. The result is we have this product that’s water and dust resistant. I think the sound that comes from it is so surprising for a form factor of this size.

Pakula also sat down with Katarina Mogus for an interview, where he discussed how the iPad mini fits into a world where iPhone Duo also exists:

What we love about the iPad mini is it’s really the full iPad experience in the palm of your hand. That gives you access to a million+ apps in the App Store. It’s got incredibly powerful creative accessories like the Apple Pencil Pro. And it’s got the advanced multitasking of iPadOS 27.

It is really incredibly universal. And honestly, with all these updates, all of those experiences just got so much better.

You can watch both interviews below. The new iPad mini is available to pre-order now, with the first orders arriving on November 6.

#3407. Apple cuts App Store commission in Taiwan following regulatory discussions [U]

Apple today announced that it is lowering its standard App Store commission in Taiwan, following discussions with the country’s Fair Trade Commission. Here are the details.

Over the past year or so, Apple has faced mounting regulatory pressure on several of its App Store practices and rules worldwide, particularly those related to app distribution, payment processing, commission fees, and alternative options for developers.

In Japan and Brazil, in response to local competition rules and investigations, the company introduced alternative app marketplaces, third-party payment options, and revised commission structures.

In the European Union, Apple recently overhauled its App Store fees and business terms to address concerns raised by the European Commission following a lengthy back-and-forth over its compliance with the Digital Markets Act.

Just last week, an Australian federal judge ordered Apple to allow alternative app distribution and payment methods following its years-long legal battle with Epic Games. Apple plans to appeal.

And yesterday, South Korean regulators fined Apple approximately $15.5 million and ordered changes to its App Store policies over payment restrictions, app review practices, and discriminatory commissions.

Now, Taiwan is joining that list, though the changes announced today are considerably narrower. Apple today informed developers that, starting this Saturday, October 31, its standard commission on paid apps and in-app purchases will drop from 30% to 26% in the Taiwanese iOS and iPadOS App Store.

Apple said the change follows discussions with the Taiwan Fair Trade Commission, and added that “signing the updated terms by October 31 is not required to receive the benefit of these commission rate changes starting that date.”

The company also updated its Apple Developer Program License Agreement to reflect the new terms, with translated versions expected to be available within the next month.

To read Apple’s full announcement, follow this link.

Update: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:

“We’re making updates to the Taiwan storefront of the App Store following constructive discussions with the Taiwan Fair Trade Commission. These changes reflect our ongoing commitment to providing developers with a thriving marketplace and ensuring the App Store remains the safest, most trusted platform for users. We will continue to equip developers with the tools, resources, and support they need to build, grow, and scale successful businesses on the App Store.”

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Foggy, cold, and hardscrabble, the community of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland, is the perfect spot for ocean-borne horror in Netflix's Below. This sense of place sets the series apart, though the characters who inhabit it are equally fascinating. Led by Josh Hartnett’s grounded performance as Calvin, the show has atmosphere for days, and a creepy and compelling story that effortlessly balances chills and deep emotional beats.

If you ate this show up like a voracious sea creature and you’re craving more slow-burn, deeply human horror (and you’ve already explored all the similar streaming series out there), it’s time to move on to feature-length terror, and there's one classic movie that fits the bill.

When it comes to kindred sea monster stories, Jaws is the obvious choice. Seaside setting? Check—a pre-glam Martha’s Vineyard stands in for Amity Island, with beautiful beaches and crashing waves to spare. A tight community under threat? Check—Amity Island feels like a very real place, and its citizens have concerns and grudges as legitimate as Calvin’s in Below. Shocks and frights? This is Jaws, a film that transformed the entire business of blockbuster movies, renowned to this day for its masterful depiction of a relentless natural force threatening an entire town.

The basic story also echoes Below's: When a young woman is killed by a shark during a night swim, Amity Island Police Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) tries to close the beaches to protect the public, but Mayor Vaughn (Murray Hamilton) refuses, as Amity Island depends on the tourist trade for its survival. After a young boy is killed, Brody teams up with shark hunter Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) to hunt the beast, and the three soon find themselves in over their heads as they discover how big and relentless the shark really is. Both stories share themes of economic necessity trumping safety in a changing world and concepts of a small group of people fighting a terrifying natural threat.

Like almost every horror film or series since 1975, Below owes a debt to Jaws in terms of storytelling and technique. From the isolated, ocean-centric setting (and monster) to the way Below shows you only flashes of its central terror, if you enjoyed the series, you will absolutely love the classic that influenced it. Stream Jaws on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Already seen Jaws, or rewatched it, and still in need of more terrifying movies in the same vein as Below? Here are a few more movies that you’ll love.

The Bay takes a different approach to its scares than Below—it’s a found-footage horror film. But it shares the remote, water-centric setting, the focus on a small community, and a story that pulls from the terror of a fundamental element—water—being polluted and corrupted. In the coastal community of Claridge, Maryland, citizens fall severely ill and begin dying in large numbers, sparking chaos. As investigators race to discover the source of the affliction, the carnage gets seriously gnarly. Just like in Below, the ultimate threat stems from the way people recklessly abuse the world we depend on for survival, and the local residents are center stage in the fight. Stream The Bay on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

One aspect of Below that resonates strongly with viewers is the human element; the Penney family’s internal tensions feel earned and real, and the way the larger community struggles with several existential crises is messy in a gloriously human way. The Host is also about a family struggling against a horrific, waterborne monster—when a mutant creature attacks a crowd near the Han River, Park Gang-du loses his grip on his young daughter, and she’s snatched up by the monster. But when Gang-du receives a phone call from his daughter telling him she’s still alive but trapped with the creature in the sewers, his family escapes quarantine, gears up, and goes after her, no matter the odds (or the corrupt government agencies standing in the way). Stream The Host on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Based on H.P. Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Dagon begins with four friends on a boat off the coast of Spain. When a storm wrecks the boat and injures one of them, a couple—Paul and Barbara—travel on foot to a nearby village to seek help. What they find instead is a terrifying place paying the price for worshiping a demon named Dagon in exchange for wealth and safety—but at a price that slowly rose, eventually transforming the villagers into something inhuman. Just like Below, the movie explores the choices communities make to survive, and the personal costs that aren’t always clearly understood. Stream Dagon on The Roku Channel or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you loved Below’s foggy, liminal feel and the constant dread of what might be lurking in the mist or under the waves, unseen until it’s too late, John Carpenter’s classic is a must-watch. As the small coastal town of Antonio Bay approaches the centennial of its founding, a strange fog rolls in from the sea and envelopes the town. As the body count rises, the true story of the town’s founding and subsequent prosperity is revealed—and the long-deferred price for the crimes of the town’s ancestors is in the fog, determined to find some element of justice. Stream The Fog on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

If remote communities like Snook’s Arm are inherently creepy to you, check out Offseason. When Marie (Jocelin Donahue) learns that her mother has passed away and has been buried in Lone Palm, the isolated beach town where she grew up, she’s outraged—her mother was very clear that she didn’t want to be buried there. Marie travels to Lone Palm as tourist season ends, just a day before the bridge to the mainland closes for the year, which gives the town a liminal, nightmarish aspect familiar to anyone who’s lived in a tourist town during the offseason. As a storm moves in, Marie and her boyfriend find the townsfolk behaving quite strangely—and soon, it all whips up into a maelstrom of terror that fans of Below will appreciate. Stream Offseason on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

#3403. Reddit will soon require an account for most content

Earlier today Reddit announced that it’s rolling out social media-style ‘For You’ feeds, but that wasn’t the only big news today. Reddit also now says that it’s going to start requiring a logged-in account for accessing most of its content.

Reddit on Thursday said it’s moving to become a primarily logged-in experience, marking one of the most significant shifts in its 21-year history.

Reddit has long championed the open web. Now, it’s pushing to build a more direct relationship with users while also protecting its data from increased scraping in the AI era.

Reddit co-founder and CEO Steve Huffman said in an interview that the change is being made to “improve its user experience, bolster its ads business and prevent bots from scraping its proprietary data.”

That’s going to kill a lot of their traffic from search and instantly remove a ton of content from AI summaries. Interesting move.

The plan is to start testing the new logged-in experience this quarter, but only outside the US to start. It will then roll it out more broadly around the world.

What will Reddit users without an account be able to access? Huffman acknowledges they’re still finalizing those details. Per Axios though, the Reddit homepage will still be accessible to everyone. And if you visit the site “via search engines or shared links,” you’ll still be able to access the content.

However, if you try to browse Reddit in any other way or visit a specific subreddit without being logged in, it sounds like that will no longer be possible.

What do you think of Reddit making this change? Let us know in the comments.

#3400. I Tested Strava's New Integration With Gemini, and I Have Thoughts

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

#3396. Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross Scored ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’

After rumors stirred last month, it’s official: Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross provided the score to The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, directed by David Fincher and written by Quentin Tarantino.

Reznor and Ross have scored six of Fincher’s movies, including The Social Network, Gone Girl, and Mank, the former receiving the Academy Award for Best Original Score in 2011.

The duo has also struck up a creative partnership with another director in recent years, scoring the last four movies directed by Luca Guadagnino, including Challengers and After the Hunt.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is a quasi-sequel to Quentin Tarantino’s 2019 film Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood and arrives in theaters on Nov. 25 before heading to Netflix on December 23. Tarantino will release a novelization of the Booth-centered film on Dec. 8, following the 2021 work Once Upon a Time in Hollywood: A Novel. Trending Stories Dane Cook’s Brother Robbed Him Blind. Now He’s Rebuilding His Life — And Gunning for a Comeback Yes, Matt Damon and David Letterman Were Background Actors on ‘The Gilded Age’ Season Premiere Britney Spears Says Kevin Federline and Jamie Lynn Spears Made Her ‘Feel Like a Slave’ Andy Garcia, David Foster, Paul Anka Lead Kennedy Center Honors

Brad Pitt reprises his role as the eponymous stuntman-turned-fixer and takes place in 1977, eight years after the events of Tarantino’s movie, which altered the events of the Tate-LaBianca murders committed by the Manson Family. Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Timothy Olyphant, and Yahya Abdul-Mateen II also appear in the spin-off.

As Nine Inch Nails, Reznor and Ross have kept busy. The pair released Nine Inch Noize, a collaborative record with Boys Noize, in April. Last September, they released the Tron: Ares soundtrack, which marked the first new Nine Inch Nails record in a half decade.

#3395. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

#3392. Dane Cook’s Brother Robbed Him Blind. Now He’s Rebuilding His Life — And Gunning for a Comeback

Comedian Dane Cook’s house sits perched above Hollywood like a fortress, or a prison. A $7 million modernist hillside oasis with a baby-blue pool and a view stretching halfway across the Pacific, the house is Cook’s prized possession. He bought it back in 2008, in the boom years, when he was at the height of his career: selling out arenas, breaking chart records — and still a few months away from learning that his brother had stolen nearly every cent he’d earned. But we’ll get to that.

If “Dane Cook” is a name you haven’t thought about for a couple of decades, you wouldn’t be alone. For a period in the mid-2000s, Cook was the pinnacle of the comedy world. His résumé is like an aughts time capsule: one of the first comics to predict the power of social media, who harnessed millions of fans via MySpace; headliner of big Hollywood comedies opposite Jessicas Alba and Simpson; star of an HBO documentary series that aired after Entourage. In one 18-month stretch, Cook released an HBO special, dropped the highest-charting comedy album in 28 years (which eventually went double-platinum), hosted Saturday Night Live — twice — and sold out two shows at Madison Square Garden on the same night. “I had a great run,” he says with a grin.

Yet even at his apex, Cook was often the punch line — his very name a synonym for “overrated douchebag hack.” Other comics couldn’t stand him — partly for artistic reasons, and partly because they were jealous of his success. As a performer, he was always more energy than craft — cannonballing around the stage with his spiky hair and pre-distressed jeans, consonants popping like they were on creatine, sprinkling his Seinfeld-style observational bits on parking garages and mini golf with punchlines about blowjobs and tits. (Sample joke: “When you’re with somebody awful — I call that a relationshit!”) And no one could touch him.

Comedian Nikki Glaser was a huge Cook fan who once planned a girls’ trip to Las Vegas in college just to see him perform. “He was the biggest comedian in the world when I was starting out, so his influence was undeniable,” Glaser says. “There are still so many comics today who remind me of Dane, whether or not people remember him for it. He presented like a dumb frat bro, but he would sprinkle in phrases and new groupings of words that illustrated his point almost poetically. His comedy was almost musical — people would put it on at parties to just hang out to. To this day, I don’t know a comedian my friends listen to like we listened to Dane.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

But even as Cook stood astride show business, his life was secretly being dismantled under his feet. What he didn’t know was that his half-brother, Darryl McCauley — who’d served as Cook’s business manager since before he was famous — had been embezzling from him for years, possibly decades. It all came crashing down in 2008, when Cook got suspicious and started asking questions, and McCauley went on the run before being arrested. When the Massachusetts attorney general’s office finished their forensic audit, they put the total theft around $12 million. And that’s just what they could prove. Cook thinks it might be double that.

Cook avoided talking about it in public for years, for a variety of reasons. He was devastated, he was ashamed, he couldn’t figure out how to make it entertaining. But now he has a documentary — Funny Money, streaming on Netflix starting Nov. 6 — that details the whole sordid tale for the first time. “There was a hope and a concern,” Cook says of the film. “The hope was that this was a true-crime story that’s funny. The concern was that I’m a sad clown. I cried more [doing the film] than I did in therapy. So there’s really some anxiety that you see me like this.” Related Content Dane Cook’s Brother Stole $12 Million, Then Disappeared After Prison Release The Best Tech and Home Audio Gifts From Marshall and Google The Wait Is Over: Parke's NYC Mocknecks & Big Apple Merch Are Finally Here Steel Guitars by the Dozen: A Cultish Concert Pays Tribute to the Most Country Instrument of All

Cook, 54, is sitting in his home office, full of platinum records and framed magazine covers — a shrine to his fiveish-year peak. He’s wearing Earth-tone Nikes and a fitted brown polo, his highlighted hair both thicker and more kempt than it used to be. The shelves behind his desk are filled with fun nerd memorabilia, like an Obi-Wan Kenobi toy and a still-unboxed Wolverine.

As a kid, Cook used to spend hours playing with these toys — Stormtroopers battling G.I. Joes, Chewbacca fighting Doctor Doom. “But it was never ‘evil and bad’ for me,” he says. “It was always ‘misunderstood.’” What was Darth Vader’s trauma? What if Cobra Commander just needed a friend? “I was the only person watching Die Hard like: ‘But what happened to Hans?’”

For the past two decades, he’s been trying to figure out the same things about his brother. “Sometimes I sit and wonder, ‘Who is Darryl?’” he says. He shakes his head. “I don’t know.”

COOK GREW UP IN Arlington, Massachusetts, a working-class suburb of Boston. “I was very much a wallflower introvert,” he says. “A lot of anxiety. Mama’s boy.” He had cystic acne that left deep scars on his face. This is why he always moved around so much onstage — what he calls “the whirling-dervish thing.” “I just didn’t want you to look at me,” he says. “If I don’t stay still, then you won’t key in and go, ‘You’re ugly.’”

Darryl was seven years older — his half-brother from his mom’s first marriage. They were never extremely close on account of the age difference, but they did share a bedroom, and they did hang out — playing R.B.I. Baseball on Nintendo, or raking the leaves while the other held the bag. Darryl was a manager at Burger King and hired Cook to work the drive-thru.

To this day, Cook has never had a drink or done a drug in his life. That’s probably because his dad was a violent alcoholic. The house was “a place of mayhem,” he says: shouting matches, wall-shaking fights, and one harrowing incident when he was 14 involving a kitchen knife that ended with his father being arrested and leaving the house. Cook says he was never a target of the abuse per se, so Darryl didn’t protect him. But just his presence helped Cook feel safe. “I remember so many nights, looking over at him as I was going to sleep,” Cook says. “Just happy he was there.”

Not long after his 18th birthday, Cook started doing standup around Boston. From there it was a long slog to overnight success: six years of living at home, doing shitty gigs at laundromats, Chinese restaurants, and open mics. “I’d spend more on gas driving my mom’s 1978 Lincoln to Maine and back than I’d even make,” he says. “A Tuesday night meant hoping you’d get up at Nick’s Comedy Stop next to the Combat Zone, where maybe I can make a couple prostitutes laugh on the way out.” Eventually he got successful enough to move to New York, and later L.A., where he landed such glamorous jobs as half a season on an ABC sitcom starring Betty White and a Dennis Rodman movie that grossed $292,000 worldwide.

Meanwhile, Darryl — who’d dreamed of being a state trooper but failed the test — was working as a corrections officer at Walpole State Prison (now called MCI-Cedar Junction), a maximum-security facility near Boston. (You might know it from The Town.) “It was a scary place,” Cook says. “I hated that he worked there.” He started plotting how to get Darryl out. “I’m incorporated now,” he recalls thinking. “Maybe at some point I can turn this into a regular around-the-clock job for us.” Then a month later, Darryl was viciously attacked by an inmate. “Some old guy put a can of corn niblets in a pillowcase and boom — cracked Darryl’s head open,” says Cook. “I go see him in the hospital. My mom is terrified. We’re all terrified. That’s when I said, ‘I want you to quit and come work for me.’”

In the beginning, Darryl was more like an assistant: paying the car insurance, boxing up CDs to ship out, selling merch at shows. But as the checks started getting more zeros, the job got bigger. Darryl became Cook’s business manager, handling operations at his company, Great Dane Enterprises, complete with a $150,000 salary. Cook says he had no reservations about giving control of his finances to someone relatively unqualified. “I felt like, he’d believed in me,” he says. “We’d gone through a lot of crazy shit together, we got out of that house, we have some normalcy and an income now. We would sit at dinner and be like, ‘This feels good. Cook-McCauley brothers for life.’

“And there was a certain safety,” he says. “Me already seeing some of the piranhas in this town, and the bad language in the contracts, I’m like: ‘But I’ve got my brother looking out for me.’”

Darryl didn’t show Cook his financial statements. Instead he would create Excel spreadsheets with “summaries” of everything going in and out. Cook says he never questioned them. For one thing, he has “dyscalculia,” the numerical version of dyslexia. (“I see numbers and they just spin around.”) Darryl also kept it low-key. “Same pair of dirty sneakers. No frills,” Cook says. “Anytime I would say to him, ‘Is there anything you want or need?’ he was like, ‘No.’” (In hindsight, that’s probably because he was stealing all Cook’s money.)

And ultimately, Cook says, he never really cared about the money. “I just love the game,” he says. “I can’t tell you how many times I’d leave a gig and they’d call me at home and go, ‘You know you forgot your check?’ So no, I didn’t ask. I believed the statements.”

‘FUNNY MONEY’ TAKES A WHILE to get going, with its first third chronicling Cook’s long rise, but when it finally drops into gear, it’s compelling — especially as it catalogues the breadth and depth of Darryl’s deceit. Cook still isn’t sure when it started, but it grew exponentially. In 2004, Darryl was writing himself checks for $22,000 here, $31,000 there. Two years later — Cook’s commercial zenith — Darryl was making deposits as flagrant as $780,000 and $995,000. As Cook’s (legit, later-hired) business manager says in the film: “There wasn’t even an attempt to hide it.”

By the fall of 2008, Cook decided to transfer all his business dealings to a more established firm. The new business manager kept asking Darryl for his files; Darryl kept ducking him. Soon he stopped returning the manager’s calls. Then he stopped returning Cook’s.

In a joke from his 2003 album, Harmful If Swallowed, a girl tells Cook that all men want is sex. Not true, he says: “Any guy here — if they had the choice — would rather be part of a heist.” The Darryl story also ends with a heist — this one in broad daylight.

In December of 2008, McCauley walked into a Bank of America in downtown Boston with a check from Cook’s company made out to himself for $3 million. It also had Cook’s forged signature. Incredibly, the bank cashed the check, and McCauley stuffed the cash into literal duffel bags, which he loaded into a rented Escalade and drove away. A final $3 million fuck-you.

Increasingly frantic that he couldn’t reach Darryl, Cook went to a bank branch near his house. A sympathetic employee pulled up his accounts. One had $110,000 in it. Another was empty.

“I’ve never been in a plane crash,” Cook says. “But I imagine when everything’s rattling, and you start to hear unusual sounds, and things are tearing apart — that’s kind of how I felt. My legs go out from under me. I’m howling with sadness. Because I know my best friend in the world has done this.”

“It was a shattering unlike I ever imagined,” he continues. “I’ve had a couple of bad panic attacks in my life — like, catatonic. Nothing compared to what I felt that day. I could cry right now thinking of it.”

Cook called the cops, who brought in the FBI. Darryl went on the run — a wild sequence in the doc — and was arrested by Massachusetts State Police a few weeks later. His wife, Erika, was also arrested; when police searched the couple’s home near Boston, they found $800,000 in cash stashed in a wall safe. A separate search of their beach house in Maine turned up hundreds of thousands more: bricks of cash in Tupperware tubs of tomato sauce hidden in the freezer; $90,000 in a box of Bagel Bites; $150,000 buried in the dirt of a potted plant.

Investigators later found that the couple had spent $5 million on real estate and investments and $500,000 on jewelry. There were also vacations in Ireland, a time-share in St. Kitts, and his-and-hers Cadillacs, along with $2.7 million in cashier’s checks that were never accounted for. “I think it’s way more than the $12 million,” Cook says today. “I’m thinking $17 to $22 million is really the number.”

McCauley pled guilty to 27 counts of larceny, three counts of forgery and one count of embezzlement. He was sentenced to six years in Walpole — the very same prison where he’d worked as a guard. Cook, meanwhile, was very fucked. Not only was all his money gone. He also owed the IRS for the taxes Darryl hadn’t paid — a staggering $6 million with interest.

What Cook did next was truly impressive. He still had about $300,000 in stocks that Darryl somehow hadn’t touched. He used the money to book himself an arena tour, renting the venues out of his own pocket. “I take the door, they take the food, I sell my merch,” he says. “If I’m renting a $35,000 dollar arena, there’s nights where I’m walking out with $350,000. I was like, ‘I’m gonna go down maybe. But not because of you.’” He spent the next two years crisscrossing the country, playing a hundred-plus shows, often back to back to back. And by the end, “I’d made everything back that they told me he took.”

That was the financial hole. The emotional hole took much longer.

“The humiliation was way more damaging than the theft,” says Cook. “All my childhood stuff I thought I’d overcome, all the insecurity that was still there but shielded by success, all the self-loathing I felt as a kid — it all came back. I’m on the school playground that I thought I got away from, and everyone’s looking at me going, ‘This fucking idiot. What a moron.’”

He couldn’t write any jokes or get onstage for a year. “I was bad, man. The ruminating was really bad. All through the night. I was trying to find girls to spend time with — just unhealthy. Sex. Trauma dumping. It’s love, and it’s temporary, and then it’s rinse and repeat, another night.”

To make matters worse, this was all going down when Cook was grappling with multiple other catastrophes, both personal and professional. A couple of years earlier, he’d lost both parents to cancer within a span of nine months — a double dose of tragedy that initially brought him and Darryl closer, but ultimately made their estrangement even more painful. Around the same time, Cook was famously (and, in hindsight, unfairly) accused of joke-stealing by a pre-disgraced Louis C.K., leading to a pile-on of haters and internet stand-up police. Not to mention the normal backlash and decline he was already facing from overexposure and his defiantly un-P.C. shtick.

“I’m just spinning,” Cook recalls of this time. “I’m no longer in vogue. Also my parents have passed, and I’m probably ignoring that and not grieving. I’m doing sets at night because it’s alleviating the sadness of the day.”

One of his first shows back was a disastrous, rambling set at the Hollywood Improv, where other comics described him as “spiraling” as he reportedly told “jokes” like: “Go fuck a dirty whore. That’s the best therapy.” Eventually he realized he needed actual therapy. “It was like a year of twice a week,” he says. “Brick by brick. Figuring out again how to move in the world.”

It’s hard not to notice that Cook’s trajectory changed drastically after Darryl’s betrayal. Since 2009, he’s done just two stand-up specials and only a handful of acting gigs (including four episodes of a sitcom that got canceled before it aired). It’s been seven years since he appeared on TV or film at all. From the outside, it looks like his life got derailed and he never got it back on track.

Was it just the natural cycle of fame? The more intellectual turn stand-up took in the 2010s? Or does he blame his brother for that?

“I did blame him for a while,” Cook says. “I knew I was at the end of a run in my career — I’m cooling off. At that point where the pendulum naturally swings and everything slows down, I didn’t have the bandwidth to untangle the knots. But also, being realistic,” he adds, “I wasn’t putting up, like, Sandler $100 million movies. I was hitting doubles.”

For years, Cook struggled with how to tell the story. He wrote a few bad jokes about it. (“My brother was a prison guard. I hired him to protect my money, not help it escape!”) He even tried some material out on his therapist. (“Man. Worst audience. The stonewalling I took on some of my gems…”) For a while he thought about doing a one-man show. But he could never figure out how to get into it all while still delivering for his fans. “They’re there to see me do what I do,” he says. “I wasn’t ready to bum them out.”

Then in 2019, he talked about it on a podcast for the first time, and it unlocked something. Soon after, he got a call from the documentary’s producer offering him a million dollars.

There is, of course, one big, Darryl-sized hole in the film. McCauley turned down multiple requests to be interviewed by the filmmakers. Cook even offered to drop his $12 million restitution claim in exchange for a face-to-face sit-down; Darryl declined. According to Darryl’s LinkedIn page, after his release from prison, he worked for six months at a Home Depot, three years at a grocery store, and five years as a driver for FedEx, before entering “semi-retirement” in 2024. His bio says he “possess[es] strong judgement and decision making skills.” And in the “Skills” section, he lists one: “Finance.”

Cook says he’s never tried to reach out to his brother. He seems to be waiting for Darryl to make the first move. Even 17 years later, he sounds freshly wounded, yet surprisingly open to reconciliation. “Even in this doc, there’s some version of a love letter to my brother,” he says. “Like: ‘You did a lot for me. We did a lot together. Why are you dumb?’”

Cook claims — incredibly  — that if he could go back, he wouldn’t change a thing. “I feel like it’s all brought me to the best of my life,” he insists. “Where I’m at right now is way more interesting than anything that would have happened, had nothing happened.”

“But I do miss my brother sometimes,” he adds. “I miss that guy I game-planned with. That I made those first flyers with back in the day. A million memories of high-fives and bad fast food and driving to gigs. It was cool having an older brother. If I had a time machine, I’d probably go back and throw one more hug on him.”

Just a few months ago, his younger sister Courtney got a DM from Darryl. It was the first time any of them had heard from him in decades. The message, says Cook:

“‘Everybody’s wrong. It was $12.8 million.’ With a money bag emoji.”

LATER THAT NIGHT, COOK rolls into a theater in Santa Monica for the documentary’s premiere — the first time he’s seen it with strangers. Friars Club roastmaster Jeff Ross is in the house; Cook’s pal Dave Chappelle was going to come, too, but he had to bail last-minute. Seated next to Cook is his wife of three years, Kelsi. She’s 26 years his junior — they started dating when she was 18 and he was 42 — but at least Cook jokes about it. (Goes one bit: “People are like, You’re robbing the cradle. I’m like, Relax. She hasn’t slept in a cradle in nine years.”)

The audience is admittedly full of friends and fans, but the movie goes over great. People laugh and gasp in all the right spots. Ross uncorks a few nice heckles. Afterward, Cook is beaming. “Putting up a win with the worst moment of your life is fucking awesome,” he says. “I have regained the narrative that was hijacked from me.”

Earlier, in his office, Cook talked about the future. He hopes the documentary will be a “catalyst” for his career. He’s been inspired by seeing Chappelle and Chris Rock still touring and directing films, and says he’s hungry to get back to that level. “I belong there,” he says. “That’s the class I put myself in.”

He’s been getting in shape — preparing his mind and body. Kelsi is a certified Pilates trainer and fitness instructor, and she has him on a strict 2,000-calorie diet, doing an hour of Pilates and swimming every morning and in bed by 8 every night. He sounds like a prizefighter training for a comeback.

Can he make one? Who’s to say? Flip phones are cool again — why not Dane Cook?

“I have always been rooting for Dane,” says Nikki Glaser. “I’m sure his downfall was schadenfreude for a lot of comedians, but I think the comics at the top now owe him a lot. There’s been a stand-up boom since he showed up on the scene that hasn’t really dropped off. He made it popular, he made it sexy, and he changed the scale at which it could be done. And he’s still got it.”

Lately Cook has been taking meetings, trying to get some momentum back. He says he recently landed a role on a prestige drama from “one of the greatest producers of all time.” He wrote a book about his story and has a new hour of stand-up that he calls the best he’s ever done. His misfortune is already opening doors.

Cook is almost heartbreakingly earnest when he talks about getting back to work. “Permission to speak freely?” he says. “I’d love to work more. I’m so ready. I hope this reminds people, if you have forgotten: I’m a workhorse. I love to show up on time. I love to create an environment for the cast and crew where they go, ‘I want to work with Dane again.’ Trending Stories Dane Cook’s Brother Robbed Him Blind. Now He’s Rebuilding His Life — And Gunning for a Comeback Yes, Matt Damon and David Letterman Were Background Actors on ‘The Gilded Age’ Season Premiere Britney Spears Says Kevin Federline and Jamie Lynn Spears Made Her ‘Feel Like a Slave’ Andy Garcia, David Foster, Paul Anka Lead Kennedy Center Honors

“I didn’t work for a long time,” he says. “I hate being on the bench. I’m OK with whatever it is. I just want to be working.”

In some ways, he sounds like a kid still looking for approval. From an audience, a dad… or maybe a big brother. “When I’m on set and hitting the mark, and I get the arm around me walking out of the studio saying, ‘You brought it today’?” he says. “That’s all I want. I think I’ve got a little bit of that left.”

#3391. Report: Apple expected to ship up to 1.5 million OLED touchscreen MacBook Pros in 2027

A new report from TrendForce explores Apple’s impact on the OLED notebook market following the launch of its first touchscreen MacBook Pro, and the company’s own shipment prospects for 2027. Here are the details.

Apple yesterday announced the new touchscreen MacBook Pro, which features the same tandem OLED technology it first introduced with the M4 iPad Pro in 2024.

With two OLED layers stacked on top of each other, the technology delivers higher brightness than conventional single-layer OLED displays, while maintaining the deep blacks, high contrast ratios, and power efficiency that OLED is known for.

And while yesterday’s announcement made it official, Apple’s first touchscreen Mac has long been rumored through leaks, reports, and supply chain analyses.

In September 2025, for instance, The Elec reported that Samsung Display was preparing to begin mass production of 14-inch and 16-inch OLED panels for Apple’s MacBook Pro in the second quarter of 2026, with an estimated annual output of 2–3 million units.

Two months later, TrendForce predicted that OLED notebook market share would reach up to 12% between 2027 and 2028, partly driven by Apple’s expected adoption of the technology.

Then, earlier this year, TrendForce published an OLED roadmap predicting that Apple would introduce OLED displays to the MacBook Pro lineup in 2026, followed by the MacBook Air in 2029 (pushed back from 2027).

Now, TrendForce has published a new report with new shipment forecasts for Apple’s OLED MacBook Pro and the broader OLED notebook market.

According to the firm, Apple is expected to ship between 1.2 million and 1.5 million units of the new MacBook Pro in 2027. Meanwhile, global OLED notebook shipments are projected to “grow nearly 40% YoY in 2026, followed by another increase of more than 40% in 2027.”

Until now, the OLED notebook market has been driven primarily by Windows-based brands such as Lenovo, HP, and ASUS, which have gradually expanded their OLED offerings across different price segments. Apple’s arrival is expected to give the market additional momentum, encouraging brands to prioritize OLED models in their product roadmaps while strengthening consumer acceptance of the technology. This, in turn, could pave the way for broader OLED adoption in notebook displays.

TrendForce also notes that the “new MacBook Pro’s premium starting price of US$2,899 for the 14-inch model, coupled with its initial availability alongside existing Mini-LED models, could temper near-term replacement demand.”

As for Apple’s first OLED MacBook Air, now expected to debut in 2029, TrendForce says LG Display, BOE, and TCL CSOT are currently competing to become display suppliers for the upcoming model, as the companies continue developing their OLED manufacturing capabilities.

Finally, TrendForce projects that global OLED notebook shipments will reach 46.6 million units by 2030, though year-over-year growth will slow to 30.8%, following a peak of 42.8% in 2028.

#3390. Palm Beach Plane Crash Co-Pilot Texted Boyfriend Minutes Before Impact, Report

Nathalia Gadelha -- the 20-year-old co-pilot who died in the plane crash in Palm Beach County on Sunday -- sent her boyfriend one final text message before the fatal impact.

The New York Post says it spoke to Nathalia's stepfather, Thiago Cortelet ... who told the outlet he believes Nathalia texted her boyfriend around 12:40 PM ET ... roughly 10 minutes before the fatal crash.

Thiago says Nathalia texted her boyfriend, "I've got turbulence, I've got ice."

Nathalia's boyfriend is also a licensed pilot ... and the two made headlines over the years for how young they both were. She got her license when she was 17 and still in high school.

Her family also confirmed she had more than 1,300 hours of flight experience at the time of her death.

As we reported ... Nathalia was supporting the craft's captain, Jeff Gregory, when the plane nosedived and went down in West Palm Beach.

She was among the 9 people killed ... along with Gregory, 44-year-old Austin tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, plus his wife Helen, their two kids, and two close friends.

Nathalia can be heard in horrifying dispatch audio saying, "Holy f***, we're out of time," while a man -- presumably Gregory -- said the Lord's prayer.

The NTSB said in a press conference on Monday that they believe the plane was breaking up before it hit the ground ... and the jet experienced turbulence and icing.

#3389. One of the Best QLED TVs of 2026 Is Over $1,300 Off Right Now

TCL has been pushing the boundaries of QLED TVs, making some of the best in the market at very competitive prices. This year, the company released its QM8L model, introducing a new design and impressive features and specs to a series that isn't even their flagship. Right now, the 65-inch QM8L is $1,197.99 (originally $2,499.99), $100 cheaper than it was just earlier this month, reaching its lowest price since it launched in April, according to price-tracking tools. Larger sizes are also seeing substantial discounts.

One of the first things you'll notice about the QM8L is the “Zero Border” bezel design, which gives it a modern, minimalistic look. When you turn it on, you'll likely note how bright this TV gets, which is a huge advantage QLEDs have over OLEDs. TCL claims it reaches 6,000 nits—seeing as the brightest OLED TV on the market only reaches 700 nits, no OLED can come close to this unit's brightness. Another important spec to note here is the local dimming zones: TCL claims this TV has up to 4,000, which means it gets top-tier backlight control, limited light blooming (thanks in part to TCL's "Halo Control"), and incredible contrast levels that some might not be able to distinguish from an OLED.

As many of us won't manually calibrate our TVs, the picture modes you can switch to in the settings will be most people's go-to. This TV's "Filmmaker mode" provides accurate color and picture, and if you're a gamer, you can use the native 144Hz high-refresh rate. If you don't already have a surround sound system at home and want to keep a minimalist setup, the QM8L comes with Dolby Atmos-ready Bang & Olufsen speakers, which offer above-average audio output compared to most TVs. You can read more about these features in CNET's 8.8/10 review. If 65 inches isn't quite right for your home theater setup, take a look at the QM8L's other sizes, which are also discounted right now.

Mariah Carey season is officially underway as the Queen of Christmas makes her first holiday appearance of 2026 with a new Gucci campaign.

Christmas trees are dressed, lights are strung, and candles are lit, just in time for the singer’s arrival (to the sounds of her signature seasonal song, natch).

Gucci says the campaign celebrates Carey’s “role as a cultural icon and a fixture of the holiday season,” while capturing the “festive excitement of one of the most anticipated moments of the year.”

Of course there are plenty of presents to go around, too, with the campaign showing off the Italian fashion house’s collection of luxe handbags, shoes, and accessories for the season, all “offering inspiration for celebrations, winter escapes, and the many moments shared during the holidays,” per a release.

Carey’s Butterfly collection, meantime, includes jackets, dresses, T-shirts, shoes, and jewelry, many of which feature a custom Gucci butterfly print with crystals.

This sequined jersey top features the butterfly print against a lightweight viscose material. Gucci says the glittery piece “illuminates the holidays,” making it a festive piece to throw on for Christmas parties and New Year’s Eve gatherings alike.

This bag features Gucci’s iconic GG canvas monogram with crystal embellishments throughout. The bag comes with a chain strap and a leather strap, along with leather trim in Carey’s signature lavender colorway.

Carey fans and fashion fans alike will also want to pick up this limited-edition pendant necklace, which features a crystal-embellished GG charm, along with a crystal butterfly charm, both set on a palladium-toned chain.Butterflies, have long been associated with the singer, ever since she released her autobiographical song and album of the same name.

Carey officially kicked off the holiday season on Sunday, with her annual “It’s Time” video, marking the transition from Halloween to Christmas. This year’s video, created in collaboration with beauty brand Sol de Janeiro, has already amassed more than 4.5 million views and counting on YouTube.

Carey is also picking up streams online for her seasonal hit: According to Spotify, “All I Want for Christmas Is You” re-entered the charts at Number 37, with more than 1.8 million streams on Nov. 1.

The Queen of Christmas will also be looking to reclaim her throne at the top of the Billboard Hot 100, after Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” replaced “All I Want for Christmas Is You” as the biggest hit in Hot 100 history, at 25 weeks and counting. Carey’s song had spent a cumulative 22 weeks at the top of the charts.

What it’s like to use the iPhone Duo as my daily driver

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It’s one thing to test out a phone for a review, but it’s another to ditch your everyday phone for a foldable — especially one that still feels unfinished in some ways. Don’t get me wrong, the iPhone Duo at times feels magical, especially when I used it to binge watch Netflix on its massive screen during a flight and when regularly multitasking with two apps side by side (finally).

But during my two-week experiment of swapping out my iPhone 17 Pro Max for the iPhone Duo I did question whether I would upgrade to this device and spend $2,000 for it. Here’s what I really like about Apple’s first foldable so far, what needs work, and what it’s really like to live with it as your daily driver.

Apple has done an awesome job making the iPhone Duo as versatile as possible with its design. Unlike the Galaxy Z Fold 8, the hinge holds various angles well and the software morphs as you bend the device.

While on a recent business trip, I used the tent position to turn the Duo into my alarm clock in Standby mode. I also like to use the tabletop mode for FaceTime calls, as I usually like to pace around the room while I talk. My family likes to say I have “ants in my pants” so this helps!

iPhone Duo: up to $1,200 off w/ trade-in + unlimited @ T-MobileT-Mobile is knocking up to $1,200 off the iPhone Duo when you switch and bring your number or when you trade-in an eligible phone and sign up for a qualifying plan. The iPhone Duo features a 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR display (1,878 x 2,670) and a 5.4-inch Super Retina XDR outer display (1,398 x 2,034). It houses Apple's A20 Pro chipset, 12GB of RAM, 256GB of storage, and two 24MP front cameras. Rear cameras include a 48MP main (f/1.6) and 48MP ultrawide (f/2.2). In our iPhone Duo review, we called it the best designed foldable yet thanks to Apple's combination of polished design, robust software experience, and enhanced durability. Price check: $1,200 off @ Verizon | $1,200 off @ AT&T

I just traveled back from Los Angeles for the Apple “Pro and Tell” event, and the in-flight internet was so slow I just gave up on doing work. (Come on, Starlink!)

So instead I sat back, relaxed and caught up on ‘The Diplomat.’ It was awesome having a 7.6-inch screen at my disposal to watch the intrigue unfold. And I got really sucked into the action during a particularly perilous episode, with rich colors and lots of detail.

Another plus is the YouTube TV app. I love being able to watch four channels at once in a grid view, just as you can with Android foldables.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

Yes, it’s long overdue, but I really appreciate being able to run apps side by side. For example, I get emails all the time about upcoming meetings and appointments, and I like being able to pull up Gmail in one window next to Google Calendar in another. It just makes my day easier.

I also upload images all the time to our dedicated photo room in Slack, and it’s great that I can just drag and drop images from the Photos app into this chat. Plus, you can just tap the middle of this split view to save the app pair.

If you’re addicted to doom scrolling, you might not want to get the iPhone Duo… It’s that addictive. Videos look pretty good on the cover screen, but on the big screen they’re way more immersive in portrait mode. And it’s especially cool that you can see the comments on the right when in landscape mode and they stay up as you keep scrolling.

I’ve been generally impressed with the iPhone Duo’s cameras, despite the lack of a dedicated telephoto lens. For example, the Duo took a gorgeous shot of the Los Angeles skyline just after sunset with deep blue, orange, yellow and red all coming through.

The iPhone Duo also did a great job of taking this shot of pumpkins in a large cornucopia, bringing out a surprising amount of detail in the shadows.

One of the benefits of the iPhone Duo is that it’s compact enough when closed that you can slip it into your front pocket. And it fits just fine. But I noticed while walking around that it weighed down that pocket.

The actual weight difference isn’t huge at 8.96 ounces (254 grams) for the iPhone Duo versus 8.22 ounces (233 grams) for the iPhone 17 Pro Max, but it’s enough to be noticeable and a bit annoying. I had to tighten my belt an extra notch so my pants wouldn’t fall down, and in many cases I wound up putting the Duo in my back pocket instead.

I give Apple some credit for making Split View multitasking on the iPhone Duo so intuitive. You just swipe up on an app and park it on the left or right side, then add another app.

However, the moment you flip from landscape to portrait view the app pair goes away. This is not the case on Samsung’s Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra. The only multitasking you can do in portrait mode is putting a video window on top of another open app.

I really loved reviewing and showing off photos I took on the iPhone Duo on its big display, but taking photos feels awkward. And it’s not just because the display is so large. I actually would like a large viewfinder at times.

The problem is that the Duo takes portrait photos in landscape mode and landscape mode pics in portrait mode, which is counterintuitive. You get used to it but it’s disorientating at first.

If I was designing the iPhone Duo 2, the first thing I would do is move the volume buttons. They’re on the top of the phone, which I find awkward to use. It’s not too bad with the phone closed but it’s of a stretch with the main display open. Personally, I would rather lose the Camera Control button or put that up top instead.

While many developers have been updating their apps for the iPhone Duo at a fairly fast clip, I’m bewildered that so many apps are not optimized at all.

For example, Google Calendar is a downright disaster on the iPhone Duo. There are huge black bars on the left and right side. The same thing goes for Google Drive. Google has optimized other apps. For example, YouTube and YouTube TV show the whole screen.

But even Gmail is half-assed on the Duo. It fills the display but you don’t get a two-column layout like you do on the Galaxy Z Fold 8. LinkedIn is another example. You would think they would have updated their app by now.

I can see why Apple chose to move the dock to the right side and menus and controls for apps. With such a wide front display, it would be tricky to reach across to the bottom left, for example. But that doesn’t mean this UI change is a success.

When you have just 5.4 inches to play with, taking up that much room in every app seems like a waste. Check out Instagram, for example, which has been fully optimized on the iPhone Duo. The right-hand strip means there’s less room for watching videos compared to the Fold 8.

The situation is even worse with apps that have a black bar on the right side, such as TikTok. And then you have apps whose right-hand menu covers the content as you scroll. Maybe Apple should just move all the controls to the bottom and allow developers to hide them, revealing them with a swipe or tap?

After giving up my iPhone 17 Pro Max for the iPhone Duo for two weeks, I feel like Apple has delivered a foldable phone that is (mostly) well designed. I really like having a huge display on the go that folds up into a more compact design. It’s like having an iPad Mini in your pocket, even if it weighs me down a little.

I also like the quality cameras, split-view multitasking, and consuming vertical video. However, I’m pretty shocked that very high profile developers have not fully updated their apps yet, which can make the Duo feel unfinished. And I don’t agree with some of Apple’s own design and UI decisions.

Do I think you should wait for an iPhone Duo 2? Not necessarily. I think the iPhone Duo is compelling, but I might wait for Apple and its partners to work out some of the early kinks before forking over two grand.
