#3329. Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

His data systems make sure Claude’s answers are accurate

IEEE Senior Member Gurmeet Saran is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind Claude’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs.

If you’ve ever wondered how Claude and similar AI agents can answer complex questions in seconds and where they get the information, you’re not alone.

Gurmeet Saran works to find that answer every day as an engineer at Anthropic in San Francisco, the AI research company behind Claude. The IEEE senior member is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind the chatbot’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs.

Gurmeet Saran Employer Anthropic in San FranciscoTitle Member of technical staffMember grade IEEE senior memberAlma maters University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India

University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India

Safety is a priority for Anthropic, he says. According to Claude’s mission statement, the company wants the AI agent to be “genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive.” Crucial to the mission is ensuring that researchers can observe and understand how AI models behave, a challenge that is especially acute for large language models, Saran says.

“We have decent tools to monitor databases and web services,” he says, “but for LLMs, we’re still figuring it out.”

Saran’s interest in computing systems dates back to his childhood in Kolkata, where he logged as much time as he could in the school computer lab.

“I remember the first time I used one of the computers,” he says. “What struck me was that you could write instructions, and the machine would follow them exactly. No ambiguity.

After graduating from high school in 1999, he stayed in India to pursue advanced degrees. He earned a bachelor’s degree in electronics and telecommunication engineering in 2004 at the University of Kalyani. In 2010, he earned a master’s degree in software engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani.

While a graduate student, he began his career in 2007 at Yahoo as a technical lead of the data team in Bengaluru, India. While there, he encountered the project that shaped his career trajectory: working on web analytics and business intelligence reporting solutions.

“We kept running into a frustrating problem,” he recalls. “Different teams would calculate the same website metric—something like daily active site users—using slightly different logic, and end up with conflicting answers. It sounds like a small issue, but when leadership is making decisions about resource allocation and product development using that data, not knowing which number is correct becomes a problem.”

The team built a central data repository with defined metrics, essentially serving as a single source of truth. Saran created a model that defined what “daily active site users” means, breaking down which events counted, how to handle edge cases (or when standard code fails), and more.

With the new model, data teams across the company could rely on a standard method to determine the number of daily active users for the projects and sites they were responsible for and obtain comparable results using the same logic.

From there, Saran and his team built Yahoo! Digits, an internal web analytics tool used for all the company’s products.

Saran left Yahoo in 2010 to join Intuit as a staff engineer in Mountain View, Calif. He helped build the analytics infrastructure that unified data across the company’s products, including TurboTax and QuickBooks accounting software. During his tenure, Intuit developed a feature that detected fraudulent tax filings in real time. It required Saran and other engineers to build a system to protect taxpayer data while adhering to strict U.S. Internal Revenue Service policies.

“IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations.”

Saran joined Meta (known as Facebook at the time) in 2016 as a lead software engineer in Menlo Park, Calif. The company was facing controversy over its video metrics: Meta publicly acknowledged an error that caused it to overstate the number of views for posted videos.

“This wasn’t a coding bug; it was an architectural problem,” Saran says. He built a system that worked similarly to what he had developed at Intuit, whereby one single truth was defined to govern all video view metrics across the site.

That system, Metric360, eventually became part of the site’s architecture. By the time he left Meta in 2021, he says, Metric360 was being used across the company to calculate video metrics.

He left the company to become a principal software engineer at Wealthfront, a financial services company in Palo Alto, Calif. He helped build the company’s data infrastructure.

Saran joined Anthropic in 2025 as a member of the technical staff.

To describe the implications of his work, he uses a medical analogy: “Imagine a doctor is monitoring a patient’s vital signs and making treatment decisions based on those numbers. What if one or a few of the medical devices used were slightly miscalibrated? Even if most readings are fine, it’s a serious problem because the difficult decisions happen in the margins.

“It’s the same with AI systems. My job is essentially to make sure the instruments are giving accurate readings—that the data means what it says it means.”

His job comes with high stakes and complex problems to solve.

“AI agents are especially tricky to observe,” he says. “When a system is taking sequences of actions [generating conversational responses with different users], you need a way to capture what it did, what information it was working from, and whether outcomes matched what the end user expected. And you have to do all of that without exposing anyone’s private information—the systems are designed to recognize sensitive data and keep it protected as it flows through. It’s a much more demanding observability problem than anything I’ve worked on before.”

Solving for system reliability while AI is still in its early days of adoption is both Saran’s passion and the problem that keeps him up at night, he says.

“I think making AI systems genuinely auditable and transparent is one of the more important engineering problems of the next decade,” he says, “and it doesn’t get talked about as much as model capabilities do.”

“After more than 20 years of building data infrastructure across organizations like Yahoo, Intuit, Meta, and Wealthfront,” he says, “I wanted to contribute back to the technical community through peer review, publishing, and engaging with the broader engineering research ecosystem.”

He says he believes IEEE can play an essential role in shaping the future of AI through its standards work.

“We have standards for everything, from building codes to software testing,” he says. “AI infrastructure needs something similar, and IEEE has the credibility and the reach to do that.”

Another problem that IEEE can solve for, he says, is access: “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters, especially as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations in a few cities.”

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

#3327. WhatsApp announces four new features to make group chats easier to manage

In a blog post this week, WhatsApp confirmed that it is rolling out four new features designed to make it easier to manage group chats and keep track of what’s going on in each one. Here are the details.

WhatsApp this week announced that the filter drawer, which appears when users swipe down on the conversations list, will now include a “Mentions and replies” button alongside other filter options such as Groups, Favorites, Unread and custom filters.

Once tapped, the chat list will show only “unread group conversation[s] where you were either mentioned or received a direct reply, including @all messages,” says WhatsApp.

Additionally, WhatsApp will now let users pin messages indefinitely in group chats, rather than choosing between 24 hours, 7 days, or 30 days.

Another in-chat feature coming to groups is the ability to “send someone recent messages retroactively after they’ve joined a group just by tapping their name in the chat.” Previously, this was only possible when adding someone to a group, rather than after they had joined.

Finally, WhatsApp is rolling out group status sharing, which lets users post updates visible only to members of a specific group. Other members can view, react to, and add their own statuses, which disappear after 24 hours.

As is often the case with WhatsApp updates, it may take some time for all four features to become available to everyone. To check out the full announcement, follow this link.

#3325. IEEE Continues Preparations for the Realignment of Its Regions

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

The redrawn IEEE region map that will become effective in 2028.

Progress continues in restructuring IEEE’s geographic regions, as outlined in The Institute’s February 2023 article “IEEE Is Realigning Its Geographic Regions.”

The restructuring is defined in the image of the redrawn map in this article.

Although the new regional alignment will not officially take place until 1 January 2028, several activities have begun within IEEE Member and Geographic Activities (MGA) and across other IEEE organizational units. Within MGA, volunteers and staff have been actively addressing system enhancements, director/director-elect elections, governance updates, communications, and regional finances and offerings.

Work will continue from now until the effective date of realignment in 2028. The change will not affect your IEEE membership, nor will it change either your local IEEE section or chapter.

If you have any questions regarding the realignment, contact Reg-Realignment@ieee.org.

IEEE Member and Geographic Activities oversees IEEE membership and the activities of its geographic units worldwide.

#3323. This Handheld Vacuum Fixed My Biggest Problem With Cleaning

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

I may not be “messy,” exactly, but no one would describe me as “neat,” either. One of my biggest issues is that I tend to wait for a mess to get big enough to justify dragging out a full-size vacuum before I deal with it, because a full-size vacuum means finding the cord or the charger, wrestling it out of the closet, going room to room, and then putting it all away again. When the mess in question is still only a few cracker crumbs? Forget it—I'm just too lazy.

The solution to my laziness has been removing all the friction and hassle of my full-size vacuum, and instead keeping a handheld vacuum always within reach.

Though there are many handheld vacuums out there, I use the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, which I got from Target. It's great for quickly sucking up crumbs and everyday messes, and that's exactly the job I need it to handle. The "dual air" part is what makes it more interesting than your average handheld: It's both a vacuum and a blower, so it can pull debris in or push it out, depending on what you're dealing with. I didn’t expect to need the blower at all, but I’m surprised how handy it is for blasting crumbs out of keyboard keys or loosening up stubborn debris before I suck it up.

The result is that my apartment is simply cleaner. Not because I'm spending more time cleaning overall, but because I'm no longer letting small messes pile up into big ones. When my monthly (or quarterly) deep clean does roll around, it's far less painful, because there's so much less to deal with. Perhaps this is the real upgrade: cleaning up messes the moment they happen instead of saving them up.

I love the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, but there are plenty of similar cordless handheld vacuum and air duster combos out there, and they tend to land in a pretty similar price range. If another one catches your eye, or goes on sale, or has a design you prefer, go for it.

When comparing models, here are my handheld vacuum musts:

It should offer both vacuum and blower modes.

It should be both cordless and rechargeable. If it needs an outlet, you'll have another barrier to using it, and that defeats the purpose.

It should be lightweight and slim. You want something you can grab and use one-handed without thinking about it.

The dust cup should be easy to empty. If emptying it is a hassle, you'll use it less.

You should be able to keep it in plain sight. The closer it lives to where messes happen (the kitchen, the entryway), the more you'll use it.

I used to think a clean apartment meant big, scheduled cleaning sessions. Now I think it's mostly about making the small stuff effortless. A handheld vacuum and blower won't replace your regular vacuum, but it will make you far less likely to need it as often. If you've been waiting for the next big mess, or the next big clean, to get things tidy, consider changing the system instead.

#3322. The Key 2026 Midterm Races Hollywood Is Watching

As encouraging as polls are for Democrats, left-leaning Hollywood activists are viewing Tuesday’s midterm elections with a lot of anxiety — and just a bit of cautious optimism.

In fact, throughout the cycle, as candidates courted the industry’s deep pockets at tony backyard venues and one-on-one phone calls, the fatigue of donors was well apparent, whether that be from the crushing losses of 2024, the devastating wildfires and the industry’s production downturn.

There has been movement in the past month or so, as it became apparent that Democrats’ chances of retaking control of the House and the Senate were holding steady or improving. Watch on Deadline

That has been apparent by recent events featuring Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) and James Talarico, the Texas state senator seeking to flip a U.S. Senate seat to a Democrat. Other candidates who have trekked to L.A. include Sherrod Brown, hoping to return to his Ohio U.S. Senate seat, and Abdul El-Sayed, whose bid to hold a Michigan seat was marked by last-minute drama over the weekend, when his Democratic rival for the nomination endorsed the Republican opponent.

There is split in the industry when it comes to the race for Los Angeles mayor, with Karen Bass seeking another term against a strong challenge from Councilwoman Nithya Raman. A Berkeley IGS/Los Angeles Times poll last week showed a tie among likely voters.

Meanwhile, the race for California governor has been relatively quiet, perhaps given the sizable lead that Democrat Xavier Becerra has opened up in polling against Republican challenger Steve Hilton, the former Fox News host.

RELATED: Trump Loses At SCOTUS As High Court Rejects California Noncitizens Voting Request On Midterms Eve

Among the large donors is Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings, who has contributed more than $2.5 million to the House Majority PAC and $1 million to the Senate Majority PAC, as well as $300,000 to Hakeem Jeffries’ Victory Fund and almost $600,000 to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. On other side of the aisle, Skydance CEO David Ellison late last year gave $250,000 to Security is Strength PAC, the committee to support the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC) that is now backing his sister, Darline. Ellison gave extensively to Democrats in the last cycle, including almost $1 million to Joe Biden’s campaign, with Kamala Harris taking over the campaign after he dropped out.

That said, overall, there had been “considerable dropoff at the major donor level, particularly if measured by support for major Democratic national committees,” GLS Partners’ Andy Spahn, the political consultant, wrote via email. But there has been “high energy” at the smaller donor levels, drawing new donors and giving to candidates like Jon Ossoff and James Talarico.

Jon Vein, an entrepreneur and longtime donor and activist in Democratic politics, said activity has picked up in the past month. “People recognize the importance of taking the Senate as it relates to a whole bunch of things, including lifetime appointments to the Supreme Court,” he said.

There also has been some engagement: Mathew Littman, who leads The Working Group, which organizes Hollywood creatives, went to Michigan with about a dozen others last month to campaign with Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, and attend party rallies. He also hosted a recent Zoom organizing/fundriasing call with candidates including Brown, Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton and Texas gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa.

“We are going to do well [Tuesday],” said Littman, who runs the firm HowLitt with Dori Howard. “Compared to where we were two years ago, it is a gigantic change. One of the reasons for the change is we are running great candidates.”

He said that the level of activity still was down from previous cycles, which he attributes to “a lot of PTSD from 2024.” That trepidation, he said, might even carry over into 2028, even if Democrats have a good night.

“People are so burnt out by what happened,” he said.

Here are the races being most closely watched:

Jon Ossoff vs. Mike CollinsIndustry donors have showered Ossoff with contributions, reflecting not just his multiple trips to the West Coast but with the possibility that he will be a 2028 presidential contender (even though he denies he’s interested). His most recent trip was for a pair of Hollywood-centric events in October, including one hosted by James Costos, and contributors include Sally Field, Peter Chernin, Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Chuck Lorre and David Geffen. Ossoff is widely expected to hold his U.S. Senate seat in Georgia, and the only question is by what margin.

James Talarico vs. Ken PaxtonTalarico has raised Democrats’ hopes of flipping this Texas seat and becoming the first in the party to win election to the U.S. Senate since 1988. He has run a campaign free from much drama and focused on the baggage of his opponent. Talarico also has benefited from the publicity surrounding the FCC’s crackdown on broadcasters and the Equal Time Rule, as his appearances on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert and Jimmy Kimmel Live! were never broadcast but placed on YouTube, where they drew much larger audiences. Donors include Barbra Streisand, Damon Lindelof, Connie Britton, Don Henley, Bob Odenkirk, Marcy Carsey and Jon Cryer.

Sherrod Brown vs. Jon HustedOne of the most expensive Senate races of the cycle pits Brown against incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R-OH), who was appointed to the seat after JD Vance was elected vice president. Donors include Tom Rothman, Bradley Whitford, Herb Alpert, Peter Coyote, Lily Tomlin and Judd Apatow, while figures like Michael Douglas have donated to the Senate Majority PAC, which distributes funds across candidates including the Ohio race.

RELATED: Michael Douglas Predicts Electoral “Massacre” For Donald Trump In Midterms

Josh Turek vs. Ashley HinsonOne of the closest of all U.S. Senate races is for Iowa’s open seat, where Democrat Josh Turek faces a major challenge from Ashley Hinson. Prognosticators have swung back and forth on who has the edge, but Turek has drawn support from Lawrence Kasdan, Streisand, Field and Dayna Bochco.

Abdul El-Sayed vs. Mike RogersEven before Haley Stevens’ surprise endorsement of Rogers for U.S. Senate from Michigan, there have fissures in Democratic donor world over El-Sayed’s criticisms of Israel. Haim Saban has donated to numerous committees to help the party win back the House majority but also contributed $2 million to the United Democracy Project, the super PAC of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. The group invested heavily in Stevens’ campaign and opposing El-Sayed, and recently has started spending again in the race.

El-Sayed, meanwhile, has garnered contributions from figures including Cynthia Nixon, Susan Sarandon, Lindelof and Jeffrey Soros.

Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers has been greeted with shock and dismay from a lot of Democratic leaders, as well as industry figures who’ve been involved in races in Michigan. Littman called it “the greatest disappointment I’ve had in politics.”

Karen Bass vs. Nithya RamanUp until the Times poll, there had been much sentiment that Raman was going to defeat incumbent Los Angeles Mayor Bass, who has faced a backlash over how she handled last year’s wildfires and over the ongoing problem of homelessness. Bass has gotten a boost in recent weeks as some of her most ardent critics, including Rick Caruso, have said they would vote for her. Bass has drawn contributions from Saban, Byron Allen, Marta Kauffman, John Wells and J.J. Abrams, as well as Sony and Warner Bros. Discovery. Raman’s donor list includes Paul Downs, Dustin Lance Black, Adam Scott, Ed Zwick and Gale Ann Hurd. If the race is close, it could be days, or even weeks, before a winner is declared, given the notoriously long vote-counting process in Los Angeles County.

Other races are being watched, even if they have not drawn the level of support of other key contests. That includes Troy Jackson’s U.S. Senate campaign in Maine to defeat incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, with the Democrat drawing donors including Kauffman and Soros and the Republican collecting contributions from figures including Ben Silverman and Patricia Glaser.

California’s Proposition 40, a 5% tax on certain residents with assets of $1 billion or more, has drawn relatively little donor opposition or support in the entertainment industry, according to campaign finance records. That largely has been left to Silicon Valley, where Sergey Brin and Eric Schmidt are among those bankrolling the campaign against it, along with support for the competing propositions 41 and 42. It’s still being watched with interest — and some worry — even if the big money is coming from up north.

#3319. ‘The Remarried Princess’ Korean Romantic Drama To Release One Day Early On Disney+ & Hulu

Epic romantic K-drama The Remarried Empress, starring Shin Mina, Ju Jihoon, Lee Jongsuk and Lee Seyoung, will launch with the first four episodes on Tuesday, November 3 on Disney+ and Hulu, one day earlier than the originally scheduled November 4 premiere date.

The surprise reveal, announced during a press conference from Seoul, South Korea, is intended “as a special thank you to fans for their overwhelming support.” It follows months of growing excitement for the series, including sold-out preview screenings at the Busan International Film Festival, and the release of the show’s trailer surpassing 13 million views in the first 48 hours on YouTube and social media platforms.

The series is based on the hit Naver Webtoon of the same name that’s amassed close to three billion views to date. It follows the strained relationship between beloved Empress Navier (Mina) and her husband Emperor Sovieshu (Jihoon) of the Eastern Empire. With anxieties rising across the land, the couple’s relationship begins to fracture when Sovieshu falls in love with a runaway slave and attempts to move heaven and earth to win her heart. Unwilling to compromise her dignity, Navier acquiesces to the emperor’s request on one condition – that she be allowed to remarry rival Crown Prince Heinrey (Jongsuk) of the Western Kingdom. What follows is a tale of love, lust and regret that threatens the fate of an entire empire as Navier strives to reclaim her power. Watch on Deadline

The Remarried Empress has been adapted for the screen by Yeoh Geena and Hyun Choongyeol and is directed by Cho Suwon (Still 17, Pinocchio).

Following the four-episode premiere, two new episodes of The Remarried Empress will drop every Wednesday from November 11 through the series finale on November 25, exclusively on Disney+ and Hulu.

StackSocial has a refurbished, factory-unlocked iPhone 16e with 128GB of storage on sale for $354.99 right now, down from a $599 list price. The catch, and it's one worth understanding before you click buy, is that this particular unit carries a Grade C refurbished rating, meaning that it may arrive with visible scratches or dents on the housing. If that matters to you, you can get a Grade B-rated model for $399.99 for a B- grade or $434.99 for a B+ grade.

Cosmetic wear aside, the hardware is recent, and the 16e launched in 2025 as Apple's lower-cost entry with much of the same internals as the standard iPhone 16. But for this sale price, it's a great opportunity to upgrade your older iPhone.

#3317. Apple @ Work: Next to a growing token bill, Macs might start looking like a bargain

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Apple hardware costs more than it did a year ago, and if you have purchased a fleet recently, you are feeling it. Now, one thing I should mention: Macs have not risen in price with inflation or performance. If you think about what a Mac mini or MacBook Air cost when they launched vs. today, I would still say they are extremely affordable. With that being said, there’s a scenario taking shape in the enterprise where the price of a Mac matters a lot less than it used to. If open-weight AI models become a real part of how companies work, Apple Silicon might end up looking basically free compared to the token bill it supplements.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

Cloud AI in the enterprise is priced by the token, and that’s a fine model when usage is moderate. The problem is that usage isn’t staying light. Agentic tools that write code, analyze documents, and run multistep tasks consume tokens at a pace a chatbot never did, and the bill scales right along with them. Earlier this year, Fleet’s IT leadership research cited a company that burned through its entire 2026 AI budget in four months after rolling an AI coding tool out to roughly 5,000 engineers. That’s the risk with a variable cost by token usage. Finance is somewhat in the dark on what the number is until the invoice shows up.

Local hardware works the opposite way, where you pay once, and the cost is capped. Every hour that machine spends running a model after that costs you very little, aside from power usage.

Someone I’ve long respected, Horace Dediu, showed some interesting numbers in a recent Asymco piece that really shows the opportunity ahead for Apple. In one example, a 26-billion-parameter model used for analysis four hours a day, around 150 million tokens a month, runs $450 to $850 per user per month through a cloud provider. A 16″ MacBook Pro with an M5 Max and 128GB of unified memory costs about $6,500 and can run a model locally. That’s a payback period of 7 to 14 months. He gives a lot more examples, and it’s worth a read to see Apple’s opportunity here.

The reason Apple Silicon is so well suited to this is unified memory. On most PCs, the GPU has its own small memory pool, and the model has to fit within it. On Apple Silicon, the GPU shares the entire memory pool, so a laptop with 128GB can hold a model that would need a far more expensive setup elsewhere.

Viewed through this lens, a price increase on a Mac Studio is a rounding error. If the machine pays for itself in under a year, and Apple Silicon Macs can stay in service for four to five years, it’s practically free over a normal refresh cycle. Now, if agentic coding keeps improving at such a rapid pace, you might end up upgrading sooner than that.

All of this hinges on one assumption: the math only works if an open-weight model running locally is good enough for your task day-to-day. For a lot of everyday work, like summarizing docs, drafting, content analysis on internal data, and basic routine coding, the gap between open-weight models and the frontier has narrowed significantly recently. For the hardest reasoning and coding tasks, frontier models still lead, and that isn’t changing anytime soon.

There are other caveats, too: his usage figures in those examples are high, and a typical employee isn’t burning through 150 million tokens a month. Token prices have also been falling, narrowing the gap over time. I am really interested in a hybrid model as well. Cribl recently launched StreamAI, an AI gateway for telemetry that routes each prompt to the right model and includes built-in budget control. At JNUC 2026, Jamf showed on-device AI support that deploys models through blueprints, routes prompts through an on-device AI gateway, and governs all of it with AI policies. Apple is clearly thinking about this too. At JNUC, Apple’s Jeremy Butcher had this to say regarding cloud and on-device AI:

“We think our platform makes for the best way to do both,” said Butcher. “We continue to have these conversations, and we look forward to working with all of you to bring it to life.”

A hybrid model might be the best of both worlds, with routine work running locally and the hardest tasks routed to frontier models in the cloud. Either way, Apple is well positioned. Even with RAM and GPU shortages driving up hardware prices, the ROI on Apple Silicon looks promising if open-weight models end up handling a decent share of enterprise AI workloads. Mac prices are going up, but token bills are going up faster (even if token prices continue to fall).

#3316. The LG UltraGear 25G590B sounds like overkill with its 1,000Hz refresh rate — but after testing it, every other monitor feels sluggish

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

At the time of writing, the LG UltraGear 25G590B is the world’s first monitor with a native 1,000Hz refresh rate. That’s blazing fast, making the monitor perfect for esports gamers. The monitor itself sports a sleek and practical design, and features an adequate number of ports. The panel is bright (though it’s IPS only), and it boasts strong color coverage and accuracy. However, the FHD resolution might be a dealbreaker for some, and so might the 1ms response time. Oh, and it’s expensive, too.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Few monitors are like the LG UltraGear 25G590B. While most monitors top out at 320Hz, and some at 720Hz, the 25G590B kicks it up a notch to a whopping 1,000Hz, making it one of the best gaming monitors for esports. Strong color coverage and accuracy stuffed into a bright 25-inch panel makes for a winning combination. The monitor itself looks sleek and premium.

But is it perfect? Not really. Its FHD panel (which is the competition standard) doesn’t make the monitor an all-rounder. And while its 1ms response time is fine, many of its competitors perform far better with their 0.03ms or even 0.02ms response times. The monitor isn’t the cheapest either, priced at $999.

So, should you still buy it, despite its flaws? Find out in my full LG UltraGear 25G590B review.

Power, 2x HDMI 2.1, 1x DisplayPort 2.1, 1x USB-C (upstream), 1x 4-pole headphones/mic jack

There’s a lot to love about the LG UltraGear 25G590B, from its excellent gaming performance (bolstered by its 1,000Hz refresh rate) and its strong color coverage, to its sleek and practical design.

Supplied by: MSI | Tom's GuideCPU: AMD Ryzen 7 7700X | Graphics card: MSI RTX 5070 Ti 16GB Vanguard SOC | Motherboard: MSI B850E Gaming Plus WiFi | RAM: Kingston Fury Renegade DDR5 32GB | Cooler: Noctua NH-U12S | PSU: MSI MEG Ai1300P PCIE5 | Case: MSI MPG GUNGNIR 110R

First things first, let’s talk about the LG UltraGear 25G590B’s headline feature, and that’s its 1,000Hz refresh rate, achievable at 1080p.

That’s one thousand frames every second. Let that sink in.

In comparison, the LG UltraGear 27GX790B-B ($994) and the Sony Inzone M10S II ($1,099) hit only 720Hz at 720p. 1,000Hz is overkill for most gamers but if you’re an esports player looking for speed above all else, this is the monitor for you. Also, you’ll need a powerful machine to hit that frame rate — I’m talking RTX 50-series graphics cards, at the very least. You’ll need a GPU that supports the latest Displayport 2.1 standard, too. Our gaming rig couldn’t achieve 1,000fps in any game I played.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Even so, the gaming and visual experience was nothing short of sublime. You get a 1ms response time, which is slower than that of the Sony Inzone M10S II (0.2ms) and the LG UltraGear 27GX790B-B (0.2ms), but that’s because the 25G590B features an IPS panel versus the rival OLEDs, which shift pixel color more quickly. Though I didn’t experience much motion blur or ghosting, I have my qualms — but I’ll discuss that later in the “The Downs” section.

Back to the good things for now. In Forza Horizon 5, which is a highly graphic-intensive game, I hit 250fps while racing. This was with the graphics set to Extreme (Ray Tracing enabled and all). Movement was buttery smooth without any choppines, and it had me wondering how I’d go back after using the 25G590B. Counter-Strike 2, on the other hand, ran at 490fps with graphics set to High, and this jumped to a whopping 840fps when I dropped the graphics to Low.

Similar to the Sony Inzone M10S II, the LG UltraGear 25G590B features a range of gaming features designed for esports players. Via the OSD (On-Screen Display) and joystick, you can toggle an on-screen crosshair. The target point is then fixed in the center to enhance shooting accuracy — something I found useful in Counter-Strike 2 where some weapons lack an ADS mode. The on-screen crosshair helped me aim more accurately in both Counter-Strike 2 and Cyberpunk 2077.

There’s also a Black Stabilizer mode which boosts shadows without affecting lighter areas of the screen. You get AI Scene Optimization, too, which automatically adjusts key picture settings, like color temperature and sharpness, to match the content type — whether that’s work-related tasks, gaming, or movies. In my testing, it worked as described.

And of course, there’s NVIDIA G-Sync and AMD FreeSync for minimizing tears and lags. Overall, this is a competent and powerful esports monitor that doesn’t give you too much to complain about.

Alongside its phenomenal gaming performance, the LG UltraGear 25G590B boasts wide color coverage and accuracy, too. To my eyes, colors in Forza Horizon 5 appeared vivid — though not as vibrant or rich as on an OLED panel. Blacks appeared dark in Cyberpunk 2077 but, again, not as inky as on an OLED screen.

As you can see in the table above, the 25G590B covers 135.8% of the sRGB color space and 96.2% of the wider DCI P3 gamut, upstaging the Alienware AW2524H ($829) — also an IPS panel — in both spaces. 100% coverage is ideal, so the 25G590B does more than enough. You also don’t want coverage to reach too high, as that can then make colors appear oversaturated. None of that here, though — the 25G590B delivers a pleasing viewing experience.

I then measured color accuracy which is represented by Delta-E. It scores the difference between the source color and what appears on the monitor. Lower scores mean higher fidelity, with values near zero representing near-perfect accuracy. In my lab tests, the 25G590B achieved a Delta-E score of 0.14, which is excellent. It’s either on par with or better than its IPS as well as OLED rivals.

In addition to its strong color coverage and accuracy, the LG UltraGear 25G590B’s panel is bright, especially in its SDR mode.

In my lab tests, the 25G590B achieved a peak brightness of 387 nits in SDR and 310 nits in HDR (10% window size). Its SDR performance is better than the IPS Alienware AW2524H, and every other OLED competitor, as you can see in the table above. Low brightness is a limitation of OLED and QD-OLED panels, though, so this is expected.

In real-world use, I found the 25G590B plenty bright in both SDR and HDR modes. I wouldn’t recommend playing with the brightness turned all the way up anyway, as it can potentially harm your eyes.

Right before I started writing this review, I was testing the LG UltraGear 52G930B ($1,697), a gigantic 52-inch monitor that I struggled to carry up and down the stairs. The LG UltraGear 25G590B is its antithesis. It feels featherlight in comparison, and I was so relieved when I managed to pick it up with just one hand as it weighs just 11.46lbs (with stand).

As the numbers in its name suggest, the 25G590B is a 25-inch monitor, and it measures 22.5 x 20.1 x 8.2 inches with the stand attached. This makes it perfect for small spaces. It’s a little smaller than the 27-inch Sony Inzone M10S II, its chief rival, but the trade-off is that you’re getting a ridiculous 1,000Hz refresh rate (more on that shortly).

The 25G590B is sleek and practical. Similar to the Sony Inzone M10S II, LG’s offering features a cantilevered stand which channels the weight into the center, keeping everything balanced and resulting in the monitor using a small circular base. This also frees up space on your desk, giving you more room for freely positioning your keyboard. The stand’s height can be adjusted and the screen titled, and it can also swivel where it’s attached to the base.

Unlike productivity-focused monitors, like the BenQ Creative Pro PD2730S ($1,199) or the Dell UltraSharp U3226Q ($2,499), ports are fairly stripped-back on the LG UltraGear 25G590B — but they’re more than sufficient for hooking up your peripherals. Located next to the power port on the monitor’s rear panel, you’ll find dual HDMI 2.1 and a DisplayPort 2.1 ports, as well as a USB-C upstream port and a 4-pole headphone/mic jack.

Surprisingly, though, there aren’t any USB-A ports on the 25G590B. I don’t really have an issue with that, though, as I keep my keyboard and mouse plugged into our gaming rig’s motherboard. Hey, at least the 25G590B has a modern Type-C port and not an outdated Type-B one, like on the Sony Inzone M10S II.

Though the LG UltraGear 25G590B is powerful, it isn’t without its flaws. It features an IPS FHD panel, and its response time tops out at 1ms only. Oh, and it’s expensive!

This is a complaint similar to the one I had about the LG UltraGear 52G930B. Frustratingly, the LG UltraGear 25G590B doesn’t feature an OLED panel, and its IPS panel’s resolution tops out at 1920 x 1080 Full HD (FHD). Its IPS panel has a 1,000:1 contrast ratio which means that blacks don’t appear inky, while OLED panels typically deliver pitch-black dark scenes.

It’s also important to note that the 25G590B has a 1920 x 1080 FHD resolution. While this is the competition standard and is great for fast gaming, it falls short for everything else. If you’re looking for a monitor that can do everything — gaming and work — the 25G590B won’t be ideal. A monitor that has an FHD competition crop, like the Sony M10S II, will be more suited to at-home gamers, or aspiring esports players.

That, very nicely, brings me to my next point: the LG UltraGear 25G590B’s 1ms response time. Though that should suffice in casual gaming, high-speed camera pans and rapid movements can produce pixel trails or subtle blur. The monitor has a Motion Blur Reduction feature, yes, but it doesn’t make much of a difference aside from reducing the monitor’s brightness.

On the other hand, 0.03ms or 0.02ms response times on OLED panels offer dramatically sharper response. Combine that with better resolutions, better visuals, and better overall performance, and you’ve got yourself a winner. Again, for that reason, the LG UltraGear 27GX790B-B and the Sony Inzone M10S II make for better investments. Even the MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 ($949) with its 360Hz refresh rate would be my port of call over the 25G590B.

Finally, let’s talk about the LG UltraGear 25G590B’s price. Retailing for $999 at Adorama U.S. / £899 at Currys U.K., the 25G590B costs a lot for an IPS FHD monitor. Sure, you get a 1,000Hz refresh rate and that won’t come cheap in any world, but it’s also an IPS panel. For just $100 more, you could pick up the Sony M10S II ($1,199) which features an OLED panel and offers a 24.5-inch competition crop as well as an FHD mode.

But of course, if it’s sheer speed you’re after and you want the fastest monitor possible, $999 feels like a fair price to pay. Would you? Let me know in the comments below!

None other monitor does what the LG UltraGear 25G590B can — at the time of writing, at least. It packs a blazing fast 1,000Hz refresh rate, making it a phenomenal monitor for esports players and competitive gamers. It sports a lovely, sleek design that doesn’t take up too much space, and color coverage and brightness doesn’t give you much to complain about.

But things you can complain about? The 25G590B features an IPS FHD panel, and I really wish it was OLED and 4K — something many of its competitors offer for the same price. Also, it’s got a 1ms response time only which is fine for most gamers, but its OLED rivals offer faster 0.03ms (and sometimes even 0.02ms) response times.

If that doesn’t bother you (or you can afford it), and you really, really want to run Counter-Strike at over 800fps, then there’s no better monitor than the 25G590B.

#3315. Apple Maps begins blurring NASA, Space Force, and Air Force bases

You’re not a real space or aviation nerd unless you’ve taken to a map service and zoomed on the historic NASA launch pads or your local Air Force Bases, just for fun, you know? However, a recent change to Apple Maps now has some of those locations blurred from view, blocking anyone from seeing fighters on tarmacs or rockets on launch pads.

It probably makes sense as a reasonable security measure, why should some of the most sensitive locations to the United States be easily seen from commercial services on anyone’s phone?

Not every base we’ve checked has been blurred. Some rather large US Navy installations like Pearl Harbor, Norfolk, and Naval Station Great Lakes are left unburied. As a Wisconsin resident, I checked my local Air National Guard bases, those two have been left clear to see.

What we have discovered are now blurred are a lot of NASA and US Space Force locations, including Wallops Flight Facility, Virginia, Stennis Space Center, Mississippi, Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, and Vandenberg Space Force Base, California.

This change looks to have been rather recent, with no announcement by Apple for the change. On the contrary, Google Maps, has not blurred any of these military locations. It is presumed that Apple will continue to role out blurred map changes to more bases in the future.

Apple’s choice for which locations to blur first is interesting. Whiteman Air Force Base, the location of the bulk of the Air Force’s B2 stealth bombers, capable of carrying nuclear weapons, is logically blurred from view. Ellsworth Air Force Base, one of two state-side homes of the B-1B stealth bomber, both nuclear capable and can carry the most payload than any other US bomber, is also blurred. However, Dyess Air Force Base, the second home of the B-1B and Barksdale, home of the vast majority of the 74 year old and still kicking B-52s, are not blurred.

It’s no surprise that Cape Canaveral Space Force Station (featured image), is parent base Patricks Space Force Base, and Vandenberg Space Force Base are all blurred. These locations are home to the bulk of military owned launch pads and house some of the world’s most advanced and secretive satellites ever built.

But no need to worry too much, for now it seems that Kennedy Space Center and its historic launch pads, LC-39A and LC-39B, is not blurred. That doesn’t mean NASA isn’t on the list, Wallops Flight Facility, a primarily civil research focused air field owned by NASA is blurred, but it’s launch pads, also owned by NASA, are not.

Finally, two other locations that may be top on the list of online map explorers, Groom Lake (Area 51) and the Los Alamos National Laboratory and also now blurred.

Without a formal announcement from Apple, we aren’t sure how quickly the company plans to blur over future bases; and if it’s just highly sensitive facilities or if all government locations are on the list to be blurred.

Some questions that I now have are how navigation works on these blurred bases. Does Apple CarPlay work still? Or if military personnel and civilians working at these bases need to find a new service for on base navigation needs.

#3314. Amazon Prime Members Can Get Two Free E-Books in November

You can get thousands of free e-books over the course of 2026 if you know where—and when—to look. All year long, Amazon is offering free Kindle e-books to readers, with new opportunities popping up every month. In November, Prime members can get two free Kindle e-books from Amazon's First Reads program.

Amazon First Reads is a program aimed at Prime members that offers early access to new e-books across many genres, as curated by First Reads editors (one of many Prime Member benefits). Prime members can choose to download one free e-book every month from a rotating list—though some months that number is bumped up to two, usually with a free short novel—and non-members get them for a discounted price. These e-books can be read on any compatible Kindle device or via the free Kindle app.

Go to the First Reads landing page to see the full list of e-books available this month. Once you find a book that seems interesting, click the "Shop Now" button from the First Reads landing page. Make sure you’re not being redirected to the Kindle or Amazon mobile application, because you won't see the free book option there; instead, use your internet browser on your phone or computer.

Make sure you’re not clicking the ”Pre-order for...” button, as that will direct you to pay. Instead, click the “Read for Free” or the "Buy Now with 1-Click" button under the "First Reads" banner on the book's Amazon page (don't worry, you won't be charged). This will send the e-book directly to the Kindle linked to your Amazon account. You can see what it should look like from the screenshot below.

You’ll know you did it right when you see a “Thanks, [your name]!” order summary indicating the e-book is being auto-delivered to the Kindle Cloud Reader.

This month, you can choose one from nine new Kindle e-books, plus this month's short read. Amazon notes the genre for each of the books above the title, offering a quick way to narrow down your options. (If you hover over the "See Editor Notes" under the "Shop Now" button, you'll be able to read a short description from the First Reads editor who picked the book.)

#3313. ‘Dancing With The Stars’ Season 35 Recap: Team Dances Shake Up The Competition On Disney Night

SPOILER ALERT! This post contains details from Disney Night on Dancing with the Stars.

It’s hard to believe, but the Dancing with the Stars Season 35 contestants are in the final stretch of the competition.

Week 8 is upon us, and not only is it Disney Night in the ballroom, but we’ve also arrived at the team dances. The eight remaining couples will perform to Disney Broadway hits new and old including Hercules, Tangled, The Little Mermaid, Hamilton and Aida. And to their credit, they’re all performing two dances this week even though they have one less day to prepare, since the show was moved to Monday so as not to conflict with Election Day. Related Stories News 'Dancing with the Stars' Pro Ezra Sosa Says "My Dream" Is For Same-Sex Dance Partner: "I'm Working My Magic!" News 'The Next Pro' Waltzing To L.A.? BBC Studios Eyes Production Move For 'Dancing With The Stars' Spinoff

There’s also a very special guest just in the ballroom for Disney Night: Cynthia Erivo. She’s providing some expert commentary as a Broadway vet herself. Watch on Deadline

The two teams we’ll see take the floor tonight are Team Slaytopia and Team Wildcats. Their ranks are as follows:

Team Slaytopia: Alfonso Ribeiro, Tatyana Ali (team captain) and Jan Ravnik, Maura Higgins and Mark Ballas, Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov, and Julia Stiles and Ezra Sosa, dancing to “Zoo” from Zootopia 2.

Team Wildcasts: Julianne Hough, Connor Wood (team captain) and Rylee Arnold, Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach, Jenna Dewan and Val Chmerkovskiy, and Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson, dancing to to “We’re All in This Together” from High School Musical.

Olympian Amber Glenn with Pasha Pashkov. The Olympic figure skater and her pro partner kicked off the show with a quickstep to “A Star Is Born” from Hercules. She’s aiming for at least one 10 this week, after scoring all 9s on Horror Movie Night, so they’re going all out. They’re both going to play the titular character for this performance, and Pasha has decided Amber will have to take over as the lead for certain parts of the dance. “Mirror, mirror on the wall. Who’s the strongest of them all?” Bruno Tonioli exclaims, but he couldn’t help but point out that one tiny misstep she made. SCORE: 34 out of 40

Reality star Maura Higgins with Mark Ballas. These two are feeling pretty good after last week, but they are really trying to level up with a jive to “You Can Fly! You Can Fly! You Can Fly!” from Peter Pan. A fitting song for the woman whose catchphrase is “I tink!” But, the jive is pretty fast, and Maura is struggling to handle the pressure in rehearsals. There were a few missteps, but overall she brought that Tinkerbell spirit to the ballroom and got the audience on their feet. “It felt like at times the energy dropped and came back in. I just want to remind everyone…take care of yourself throughout this competition,” Carrie Ann Inaba said. SCORE: 32 out of 40

Actress Tatyana Ali with Jan Ravnik. The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air alum and her partner are coming off a bit of a brutal week of scoring on Horror Movie Night, when guest judge Shirley Ballas gave them a four. Tatyana is happy to be back for another week and is looking forward to proving why she’s here to stay with a contemporary routine to “Easy as Life” from Aida. Jan knows the judges will be looking for powerful emotions and an intimate connection, so he’s drilling that into her in rehearsals. It seems to have paid off, but all the judges think she needs longer lines. “You have this divine feminine energy,” Derek Hough tells her. SCORE: 33 out of 40

Actor Harry Shum Jr. with Jenna Johnson. These two were the first to receive a perfect score this season, so they’re riding a high and they also have a lot to prove with a jazz routine to “Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious” from Mary Poppins. Harry wants to infuse the spirit of Dick Van Dyke into this routine and bring a little bit of magic to the ballroom floor. They do not disappoint. Harry’s toe touch was quite impressive. “I saw all of these legendary movement-based people, and the comedy in it, the intricacy in it just blew my mind. I’m flabbergasted,” Cynthia Erivo said. SCORE: 40 out of 40

Paralympian Ezra Frech with Daniella Karagach. This Paralympic gold medalist and his partner took a little bit of a step back last week, so they’re aiming to make up for that this week with a samba to “Under the Sea” from The Little Mermaid. Previously, Daniella says they thought the samba would be off limits given Ezra’s mobility limitations with his prosthetic, but now she thinks his mind-body connection is strong enough to take it on. Unsurprisingly, she was right. “He looks like a prince and dances like a devil!” Bruno says. SCORE: 37 out of 40 (a 10 from Derek!)

Actress Julia Stiles with Ezra Sosa. These two are taking on a paso doble to “Satisfied” from Hamilton this week — the first time in a while they won’t be paying homage to one of Stiles’ own projects. The man himself Lin-Manuel Miranda is already rooting for Julia, so she’s got the wind in her sails. Now, all that’s left is to nail the intensity of this style of dance, if she can get past the intense pain in her ribs that began flaring up a few weeks ago. And she certainly satisfied the judges with this performance. “I loved it. I thought it was great,” Carrie Ann told them. SCORE: 33 out of 40

Actress Jenna Dewan with Val Chmerkovskiy. The Rookie star is getting some pointers from her Tony nominated fiancé Steven for her quickstep to “Be Our Guest” from Beauty and the Beast. Steve says it is more important for the performance to be truthful than “big,” even on Broadway. So, that’s the advice they’re using as the foundation of their routine this week. It’s a narrow needle to thread, since this is a pretty lively song, but they prove themselves yet again. “That’s what I love to see in a quickstep!” Derek proclaimed. SCORE: 40 out of 40 (their first perfect score)

Comedian and podcaster Connor Wood with Rylee Arnold. Sporting a goatee as his faux hair of choice this week, Connor must find his inner grace for a waltz to “I See The Light” from Tangled. They scored their first 10s last week, and they’re riding high, so it’s a big week for them. Of course, Connor has to call in his buddy Milo Manheim, a former DWTS contestant and the Flynn Rider in the upcoming live-action film. He’s hoping not to let his adrenaline get in the way, because this is definitely not the dance to unintentionally speed up. “The thing I was really taken by was the commitment to the storytelling,” Cynthia says. SCORE: 32 out of 40

Team Slaytopia. They’re really leaning into the zoo in Zootopia with this number. This is really the first time these celebrities will need to remain in sync and have to really block themselves with other dancers. They’re in it to win it, though. And their competition should think twice about messing with the girl power on this team. Watch out, Team Wildcats! “I had so much fun…that’s perfect. I love it. Thank you for that,” Cynthia says. SCORE: 36 out of 40

Team Wildcats. It’s always tough to go last, and this group has to follow up a dance that was pretty universally praised by the judges. However, the teams are pretty evenly balanced, which is surprising considering the team captains were the ones to decide who they’d compete with. This group is looking to bring a ton of energy to the ballroom floor and, of course, some classic High School Musical choreography. Team Slaytopia better not rest on their laurels. “I got, like, weirdly emotional watching that,” Derek admits. SCORE: 40 out of 40

The end is nigh, so unfortunately another couple has to go home this week. Julia and Ezra are sent packing.

The highest-scoring couple from the first round gets immunity for next week, but since both Jenna and Harry got perfect scores, they had to add up their total scores from all eight weeks. Harry won by just one point, so he’s in the clear! Next week is Grammy Night in the ballroom, and don’t forget the show is returning to its normal Tuesday timeslot.

#3312. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR looks awesome, but I’m not rushing to upgrade

After five years, Apple released its first major MacBook Pro overhaul since the M1 Pro/M1 Max models, and well… it was a little bit underwhelming from a design perspective. The product is incredible on many merits, but after seeing it, I’m not left feeling like I need to buy one – at least not yet.

The new MacBook Pro is substantially lighter. That’s a major improvement, especially if you’re someone who carries around a 16-inch MacBook Pro. With this new PROLED XDR generation, the 14-inch model reduced in weight by 0.5 pounds, and the 16-inch model reduced by 0.7 pounds. That’s a great deal when you’re carrying it around in a backpack or similar. The new models are also marginally thinner.

For me, though, I find myself a bit surprised by the fact that nothing about the top case design changed. The keyboard, trackpad, speaker, and port layouts all look about the same, and the chassis didn’t change shape besides getting a bit thinner. For every MacBook Pro overhaul in the past, the top case has changed in a meaningful way. With this overhaul, it really feels like more of a display upgrade that’s also accompanied by a lighter chassis.

Was there anything wrong with the current MacBook Pro chassis? Not at all. However, you could also argue the same for most design shifts in Apple’s history. It would’ve been nice to have a slightly different look, beyond the display.

This is more of a personal point. That said, I already have an M4 Pro model, and given the fact that these new MacBook Pros are substantially more expensive ($400 more compared to the miniLED MacBook Pros, which are also $300 more than they were prior to the June price hikes), I’m not particularly excited to buy silicon that isn’t the latest and greatest. The M5 family kicked off last year, and we already know M7 is coming next year.

I fully understand why Apple opted to skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max chips, but it sure does make this MacBook Pro feel ever so slightly more uninteresting.

Apple already alluded to the fact that they have more in the pipeline when it comes to macOS optimizations for touch, so maybe I’ll be wowed in the future. For now though, aside from being able to interact with the iOS simulator with proper touch, I don’t really see much of a need to have touch on my Mac.

It’s great that it’s there, and I’m certainly not disappointed that Apple added it – but I’m not yet convinced I truly need it.

None of this was to bash on the new MacBook Pro at all. In fact, I’ll most definitely be buying one in the future, most likely once it gains M7 Pro and M7 Max chips by this time next year. Hopefully touch feels more important by then. I certainly love the idea of having a glowing Apple logo again, just not quite yet – and it’s not like this product will be going anywhere if I don’t buy it during the first iteration.

I bought a ridiculously overpowered M1 Max with 64GB of memory back when they were first released, and I have zero incentive to upgrade to this day. This machine covers all my needs with ease still.

It’s also worth noting I haven’t yet seen the new display in person. It’s totally possible I’ll be blown away once I see it, but I still think I’ll be capable of waiting. Especially since my M4 Pro MacBook Pro already has a 1000 nit display, so I’m not missing out too terribly from the OLED model.

How do you feel about the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR? Will you be buying one, or are you in a similar boat as I am? Let us know in the comments.

#3311. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.

#3310. PSA: Today’s the last day to purchase discounted cushion kits for Beats 360

Apple introduced the new Beats 360 headphones about a month and a half ago. I reviewed them, and really appreciated their customizable design, the fact that they offer automatic device switching, as well as their comfort. At the time, Beats offered launch pricing on additional sets of cushions, bringing them down from $50 to just $10. After today, that steep discount will be ending.

With Beats 360, the name of the game was the customization, so the company offered steeply discounted cushions so you could mix and match your headphones and make them feel like yours.

There’s two types of cushions: Performance Knit and UltraPlush, and the sets of cushions normally cost $50. There’s a variety of color options for each cushion style, though personally I find the UltraPlush to be a must-buy.

Performance Knit is available in six color options: Black, Cloud, Pink, Sky, Navy, and Volt. The first four are headphone color-matching, and the latter two are unique options. All are available for just $9.99 for the rest of today.

UltraPlush is available in only two color options: Black and Cloud. To me, these are far more comfortable, so if you own Beats 360 and haven’t yet picked up a set of these, I’d recommend it.

The ultimate shape-shifter 🎃. Beats 360 is made to change with swappable ear and headband cushions. Special pricing ends tonight. Link in bio. pic.twitter.com/BdWjSEymLj

If you don’t own a pair of Beats 360 at all, you can purchase them on Amazon for $349.99.

#3309. ‘Jimmy’ Review: KJ Apa Expertly Channels James Stewart In An Inspiring Movie That Tells The Story The Beloved Oscar Winning Star Kept To Himself

When Kelly Stewart Harcourt (who is also an Executive Producer) was told about the idea of making a movie about her father, the Oscar winning legend James Stewart, her reaction was that it might be pretty boring since her dad didn’t live a life full of scandals, drugs, drinking or other staples of biopics about movie stars. In other words he was a straight up guy. Then she learned the pitch wasn’t to do a standard birth to death typical film in the genre, but one that focused on the period of his life of which he was most proud, his service in the U.S. military, more specifically World War II where he flew 20 dangerous missions over Europe as a combat pilot in the U.S. Army Air Corps, rising to the title of Colonel at war’s end (and ultimately Brigadier General). It was, she says, something he never spoke about to her or her siblings.

Jimmy aims to change all that and bring this largely unpublicized part of Stewart’s life to the frontlines and give it the attention it deserves. The movie doesn’t ignore completely his status as a movie star or his film career but that is just a starting off point. That aspect comes more fully into view at the end of the war with his doubts, even depression, about his ability to return in front of the cameras after director Frank Capra (who previously directed Stewart in You Can’t Take It With You, and Mr. Smith Goes To Washington) worked hard to convince the star to do a script he had, It’s A Wonderful Life. The film is far more effective when focusing on his experiences in the war and post-war dealing with what is now known as PTSD. When he’s trying to find his way and worth back into society — and Hollywood — Jimmy proves to be a cut above your average movie star biopic. Watch on Deadline

We do get a sense of the kind of fame Stewart had as the winds of war started to blow. He was a major star, even winning a Best Actor Oscar in early 1941 for The Philadelphia Story after having first been nominated for Mr. Smith the year before. But after Pearl Harbor, Stewart (played in a terrific turn from Riverdale’s KJ Apa) became among the first stars to enlist. He was already an experienced flyer, but the system tried to hold him back. MGM studio head Louis B. Mayer (Jason Alexander) attempted to convince him not to do it, saying it would hurt his career, but he didn’t listen.

Once in the military, the U.S. government wanted him only to do PSAs in order to help recruitment. Stewart was frustrated because he knew there was more he could contribute and so, in the film, he convinces Col Terrill (Rob Riggle) to give him a shot. That led to his command over a whole fleet of B-24s and hundreds of men, personally flying some of the riskier missions himself.

Director Aaron Burns effectively handles the aerial and battle sequences here giving us the real-life kind of film Stewart never really made as an actor (later he would do one, Strategic Air Command, that showed off his flying abilities).

The latter part of Jimmy is all about the production of the 1946 film It’s A Wonderful Life, in which Stewart played George Bailey, a man at the end of his rope who feels he has lost it all and even contemplates suicide until he sees what the world might be like if he had never lived at all. During the film’s production, Stewart is riddled with doubt about his own life and ability to pick up where he left off.

It is a fascinating portrait of art imitating life imitating art imitating life as Apa channels Stewart’s deep self-doubts while playing Bailey’s severe depression, the price of having given it all up to serve his country witnessing first hand the hell of war. These scenes are quite moving and well played by Apa, who not only convinces us with that famous voice of Stewart’s but also his demeanor on screen and off. It is no mere impression but a nuanced and authentic portrayal that shows us a side of the iconic man who represents the best we can be.

Among the supporting cast, Max Casella is excellent as Capra. As is Christopher McDonald ,who plays Lionel Barrymore, the Wonderful Life co-star who offers much-needed encouragement and inspiration to Stewart at a key time. Neal McDonough is also very good as Stewart’s father who also served (during WWI) and had hopes his son would follow his footsteps into the family hardware business. Among female members of the cast Kara Killmer is a love interest, Sarah Drew is gossip columnist Hedda Hopper, and Jen Lilley is Gloria, whom he would eventually marry. All have brief but nice moments.

Look closely and you might spot a cameo from Karolyn Grimes (now 86) who actually played Bailey’s youngest daughter Zuzu in It’s A Wonderful Life. Nice touch. Incidentally here is a fun fact: It’s A Wonderful Life was actually a box office flop when it first was released, even though it was nominated for Best Picture and earned Stewart a third Best Actor Oscar nomination. Of course it has stood the test of time and now is arguably the most revered Christmas movie of them all. Jimmy will give you a new perspective on it, and the man who plays the lead role, the next time you watch it. More than anything else this inspiring film reminds us that they just don’t make movie stars like Jimmy Stewart any more.

Producers are Burns, Justin Strawhand (who also wrote the screenplay), Angela Galgani Sullivan, David Cook, John Norton and Jack McClintock.

Cast: KJ Apa, Max Casella, Jen Lilley, Kara Killmer, Sarah Drew, Rob Riggle, Christopher McDonald, Neal McDonough, Jason Alexander, Julian Works

Stewart was a legitimate and modest hero, but he certainly commanded no B-52 bombers during World War II; that plane didn’t fly until 1952 and only entered service in 1955. He did, however, command (and pilot) a large contingent of B-17 Flying Fortresses in the European Theater.

I see you picked up this mistake too. However, the plane Jimmy flew was the B-24. I own a scale model replica of his plane (with nose art that says “Male Call”). It’s one of my prized possessions.

The trailer shows the b-24 with knobby tires.

#3308. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.
