#3259. Microsoft and Lumen will jointly sell networks built for AI on Azure

Lumen plans to bring its cloud networking tools to Azure, as firms struggle to link data spread across many sites.

Microsoft and Lumen Technologies are expanding their partnership to jointly sell networking to companies running AI on Azure. Lumen plans to bring its full cloud networking range to Azure. No figures or dates were given.

Microsoft and Lumen Technologies will jointly sell networking to large companies moving their AI work onto Azure, the two firms said on Monday.

Their pitch is that AI needs data from many places, such as public clouds, private data centres and offices. The networks linking them are often patchy, so the firms want customers to plan the network and the move to Azure at the same time.

Lumen, a US fibre network operator, plans to bring its full range of cloud networking tools to Azure. Its sales teams will work with Microsoft’s on deals where networking, cloud moves and AI overlap. AI has also lifted demand for fibre networks, which network-equipment maker Ciena says it can barely meet.

“AI is reshaping where applications run and how organizations use and move data,” said Katy Brown, a corporate vice president at Microsoft.

For now, customers can already buy one Lumen product, Alkira, through Microsoft’s online store for business software. Lumen bought Alkira, which lets firms manage links between clouds and offices from one place, for $475M earlier this year.

The firms also plan to explore how their networks could work with Microsoft’s tools for controlling AI agents. They gave no figures or timeline.

The deal builds on a 2024 tie-up in which Lumen supplies fibre links between Microsoft’s data centres. Azure passed $100B in yearly sales in July.

Samsung's first new tracker in three years could be right around the corner

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While the recent Fitbit Edge and screen-less Fitbit Air are the hottest fitness trackers of 2026, Samsung appears set to launch a direct competitor to the former in the near-ish future.

The Samsung Galaxy Fit 4 would replace 2024’s Samsung Galaxy Fit 3, a small tracker with a large display and support for some of Samsung’s best holistic tools, borrowed from the higher-end Galaxy Watch line.

What might the Galaxy Fit 4 bring to the table, and will it be enough to beat the Fitbit Edge, arguably the best fitness tracker for most people on the market today? Here’s everything we know (and think we know) about the Galaxy Fit 4 based on recent rumors and leaks.

The Samsung Galaxy Fit 3 debuted globally in 2024 but wasn’t available in the U.S. until winter 2025. A launch price of $59 made the Galaxy Fit 3 one of the best bang-for-your-buck fitness trackers on the market at the time, undercutting even the popular Fitbit Inspire 3.

I’ve yet to see any pricing rumors for the Galaxy Fit 4, but based on its predecessor's cost and Samsung’s history of beating the competition, price-wise, I’d be willing to bet that the Galaxy Fit 4 is a little more than the Galaxy Fit 3 (to account for inflation, at least) but still less than the $99 Fitbit Air.

Based on leaked blueprints of the device from earlier this year, first shared by Android Authority, the Galaxy Fit 4 is tipped to feature a rectangular case with a decently sized AMOLED touchscreen and a single physical button on the side, just like its predecessor and the Fitbit Edge.

In terms of display specs, the older model features a rectangular 1.6-inch AMOLED panel with 256 x 402 pixels of resolution and a max brightness of around 600 nits. What might the Galaxy Fit 4 feature?

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

My guess is that the screen size will stay the same. However, according to a recently published report from SammyGuru — which allegedly previewed an unreleased version of the companion app — the new model will have a slightly higher-res 258 × 428-pixel display than its predecessor.

In terms of brightness, given advancements in display technology over the past few years, there’s a good chance the Galaxy Fit 4 will also offer a higher maximum brightness than its predecessor for better readability in bright daylight.

What about the overall aesthetic of the wearable? A mostly aluminum case is likely, and you can also probably expect at least three color options, including black and white, with either blue or green replacing the Galaxy Fit 3's pink model.

The Samsung Galaxy Fit 4 is slated to have the brand’s GH3036 health sensor array for continuous heart rate monitoring and other holistic tracking capabilities. This information comes from Samsung’s own documents, first reported on by Android Authority.

New stress tracking and management tools could be in the cards, based on more recent insider reports; automatic workout detection is also rumored.

But beyond basic health, sleep, and fitness tracking, there’s still a lot we don’t know about the Galaxy Fit 4, feature-wise. For example, will it gain GPS for location tracking without a paired phone or NFC for contactless payments? Its predecessor lacks both, and either would be a welcome upgrade.

Like the Galaxy Fit 3, I fully expect the new model to offer safety tools like fall detection and emergency SOS, along with important health monitoring features like instant blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) readings, daily sleep scores, high/low pulse notifications, and snore detection.

Another upgrade I’d like to see is the addition of sleep apnea detection, something you’ll find on the best Samsung watches but not the Galaxy Fit 3.

Finally, the Galaxy Fit 3 is rated at an impressive 13 days of battery per charge. With the Galaxy Fit 4, battery life will likely be comparable, that is, unless Samsung outfits the wearable with a power-hungry GPS antenna.

Even if the Samsung Galaxy Fit 4 gains GPS and NFC and sells for a lower price than the competition, namely Fitbit, one major factor could ultimately limit its popularity: lack of iOS support.

While Google’s top-of-the-line wearables like the Pixel Watch 5 are Android-only, the brand’s line of Fitbit fitness trackers all play nicely with both Android and iOS devices.

This is to say, if Samsung is serious about making a dent in Google’s dominance in the wallet-friendly fitness tracker market, making the Galaxy Fit 4 multi-platform would be a wise first step.

#3256. Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Congress needs accurate technical insights

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum.

During this year’s Congressional Visits Day, Nikhil Jathar [second from left] and three other IEEE members met with Nile Whitmore [middle], a legislative assistant for Representative Greg Casar (D-Texas).

When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA.

“My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber, a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.”

What’s Your Ask? Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment.Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration.Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report.Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question.Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable.Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule.

Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:

Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”

For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits.

Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices.

On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research, and investing in STEM education. That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.”

Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.”

For Jathar’s first congressional visit, organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says.

A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour, so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too.

“If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”–Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology

The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point?

During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls.

Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge.

“When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw, designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI, which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI. This time Jathar was able to align his organization’s advocacy with his expertise and the staffer’s areas of interest.

It’s too soon to know what legislative impact that advocacy might have, but it’s the sort of informed, relevant proposal that legislative staff seek out. “The people who build trust have more cachet with congressional staff because they’ve asked for something that’s reasonably thought out,” the House Science Committee staffer says. In turn, congressional staffers can advocate better within their offices for policies brought to them by people they trust.

And talking about the issues you care the most about can deepen that trust. The House Science Committee staffer once visited Congress as an advocate before switching to the other side of the table. On that visit, as on Jathar’s, the professional society organizing the visit provided a pitch. “I was making a pitch that was given to me without a lot of personal buy-in,” the staffer says. Instead, “you should feel emotionally connected to any issue you’re advocating for.”

Jathar’s support for the open-source movement is like that. Open source gives smaller companies a foundation they can adapt and build upon, while allowing other developers to extend that work. “We can progress a lot faster,” Jathar says. “I’m not doing it only because it’s good for my business, but because I feel it’s good for any technological advancement.”

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum. He covers how emerging technologies are changing the balance of power between companies, governments, and individuals. The rest of the time, he worries about his own balance on a bicycle, skis, or the side of a mountain.

I found it difficult to get answers from legislative offices, so I'd love to hear what's missing in this story from any legislative staffers either here in the comments or at my email address (on our About page). I also know that things work somewhat differently in each country--are there readers in India or Germany or Chile who might be able to share their experiences working with lawmakers there?

As announced earlier this year, the Board of Directors has decided to initiate a process toward a potential IPO of the Grifols U.S. Biopharma business. Any such transaction remains subject to legal and regulatory requirements, internal approvals and market conditions, among other considerations. While we are currently limited by applicable laws and regulations in what we can say, we will provide updates as and when appropriate. Moving to today's agenda. Now I will turn the call to Nacho Abia?

Jose Ignacio Abia Buenache: Thank you, Danny, and thank you all for joining us today. In the third quarter of 2026, we are happy to report that we delivered strong results across our key financial and operating metrics. We are aligned with our annual plans and keeping us on track to deliver our full year 2026 guidance. Growth in our core franchises is translating into improved profitability, stronger cash conversion and lower leverage as we continue to execute on the priorities we set at the start of the year. These priorities remains unchanged, delivering sustainable growth, strengthening our financial position and advancing the strategic initiatives that will drive sustainable value creation in the future.

Let me take you through the quarter and the progress we are making on these priorities. Q3 was led by Biopharma, which grew 10.3%, supporting group revenue growth of 8.4%, both at constant currency. That commercial performance, together with continued operating discipline translated into adjusted EBITDA of EUR 538 million. and a margin expansion to 26.4% in the quarter. The contribution from the quarter brings nine months revenues to EUR 5.6 billion, up 4.6% at constant currency and adjusted EBITDA to nearly EUR 1.4 billion, with nine-month adjusted EBITDA margin at 24.8%. We remain on track to deliver our full year adjusted EBITDA margin guidance of 25%. We're also making progress on translating earnings into cash and reducing leverage.

Free cash flow before M&A reached nearly EUR 300 million for the first nine months with total net leverage declined to just below 4x. The good performance in the first nine months of the year, together with our confidence in continuing to deliver positive results in the upcoming quarters, has led the Board to announce a 2026 interim dividend of EUR 0.15 per share. Rahul will take you through the financial drivers and our balance sheet in more detail. Beyond the financial results, we have continued to move forward on several initiatives that I'd like to highlight.

In Egypt, we continue to advance our strategic partnerships, supporting the country's goal of plasma self-sufficiency and improving access to plasma-derived medicines across Egypt and the broader region. Our plasma collection volumes continue to scale in the country, and we continue to develop the supporting fractionation, purification, testing and logistics infrastructure to create an integrated platform that will support the evolution of our global sourcing model. I will return to Egypt later in the presentation. In Diagnostics, the team continued to make progress on our repositioning strategy.

Following the successful launch of Evanzys IH in Q2, we continue to advance the development of ISARD, the immunoassay platform, and MUNDAKA, the molecular NAT platform, further strengthening our portfolio and expanding our opportunities in adjacent markets. The resolution of our joint business with QuidelOrtho better positions us to capitalize on these innovation-led opportunities. While the headline growth of Diagnostics will remain negative this year due to the ending of that joint business, our underlying growth is positive, driven by solid growth in blood typing solutions and improved performance in NAT. We remain optimistic about the future of this business and are focused on strengthening our market position, driving sustainable growth and enhancing profitability and free cash flow generation.

We also continue progressing in our assessment of a potential IPO of our U.S. Biopharma business, and we'll provide updates as and when appropriate. Finally, we have successfully completed the upgrade of our ERP system to SAP S/4HANA, an important milestone that strengthens the IT infrastructure supporting our business. Together with our financial results, these highlights demonstrate our continued progress in delivering initiatives we believe create value for the business and our shareholders. Before I move on from the slide, I also wanted to provide a brief update on Canada. In mid-August, we proactively and voluntarily posted plasma collection at all our 17 donation centers there.

Recently, in close coordination and alignment with Health Canada and working together with our partner, Canadian Blood Services, we began a phased resumption of plasma collection. Throughout this period, our commercial operations in Canada have continued uninterrupted as we have sourced plasma from the U.S. to meet demand in the market. We remain committed to our long-term partnership in Canada to the importance of self-sufficiency for the Canadian market and to maintaining the highest standard of quality, donor safety, regulatory compliance and operational excellence. Turning to Slide 6. Let's take a closer look at what is driving Biopharma's performance. IG remains our primary growth engine. Industry demand continues to be strong across core markets and therapeutic areas.

And we are executing well within our markets, especially subcutaneous IG, which supports a favorable product mix. Our IG revenues grew 11.3% at constant currency in the third quarter, bringing year-to-date growth to 12.3%. Subcutaneous IG revenues grew 40.3% in the quarter, with year-to-date growth reaching 25.6%. Importantly, IG growth is not dependent on a single product, therapeutic use or treatment modality, but is supported by a diversified portfolio of IV and subcutaneous therapies, serving a broad and growing patient base. That diversification is central to the resilience of the IG franchise, as I will discuss on the next slide. Alpha-1 and Specialty Proteins also delivered a very strong quarter, up 18.2%, supported by a significant contribution from Rabies.

Year-to-date, growth reached 4.6%, consistent with the mid-single-digit growth we expect for the full year. On albumin, let me state the obvious. Performance remained challenging. Albumin declined 13.2% in the quarter and 13.9% year-to-date, both at constant currency. The revenue decline primarily reflects market conditions in China, where the regulatory environment and elevated inventories continue to weigh on selling market demand and pricing. I will discuss albumin in more detail on Slide 8. But first, let me turn to Slide 7 to discuss IG and the structural drivers supporting the continued growth of this franchise.

I would like to step back for a moment from the quarter and talk about the breadth and durability of IG demand, supported by decades of clinical experience and continued innovation. IG is used across a wide range of therapeutic areas and three of the most important conditions, primary immunodeficiency, secondary immunodeficiency and CIDP continue to deliver significant growth. Our pull-through data from 2024 through half of 2026 shows sustained growth across these key therapeutic areas, including continued double-digit growth in secondary immunodeficiencies and mid- to high single-digit growth in CIDP, including through the first six months of 2026. Primary and secondary immunodeficiencies together account for about half of the IG use in the United States.

We see growth potential in both areas, particularly in secondary immunodeficiencies, driven by factors such as the rising incidence of cancer and other conditions that compromise the immune system. Those factors, along with increasing diagnosis rates in PID, should drive continued growth in the population of patients who could benefit from IG. Our ongoing commercial efforts in primary immunodeficiencies, together with our SIGMA study with GAMUNEX-C and our EXCEL study with XEMBIFY in secondary immunodeficiencies, position us well to capture this growth opportunity across IV and subcutaneous therapies. Underneath all of this is a key differentiating factor for IG that is difficult to replicate, the multimodal mechanism of action of plasma-derived therapies.

By acting across multiple pathways in the immune systems, IG plays an important therapeutic role in a range of immune-mediated conditions, including CIDP. This differentiated therapeutic profile is relevant when considering the potential impact of emerging non-plasma technologies, many of which act through more targeted mechanisms. In CIDP, growing disease awareness creates further opportunities to identify and treat patients. Newly diagnosed patients continue to predominantly initiate treatment with IG, reinforcing its position as the first-line treatment. Through our EXPERT study, we are working to expand XEMBIFY into CIDP, with the potential to offer patients greater treatment options. Taken together, diversified and growing demand, a differentiated therapeutic profile and targeted innovation provide a strong foundation for sustained growth in IG.

Turning to albumin. China continues to be the world's largest market, accounting for approximately 700 million grams of annual demand. The market remains a strategically important one for Grifols, and our commitment to serving the Chinese patient population is unchanged. Restrictions on albumin prescribing in China have led to a downward adjustment in market volumes. At the same time, elevated inventories continue to weigh on selling volumes and pricing. When we last updated you in July, we expected market conditions to stabilize during the second half of the year. What we are seeing now is that the adjustment is taking longer than anticipated, particularly as the market continues to work through elevated channel inventories.

We are beginning to see some early signs of improvement in sell-out trends, but these have yet to translate to a sustained recovery in reported sales, and it is clear that China albumin will take a bit more time to normalize. We're navigating this situation by focusing on good execution and the commercial levels within our control. Together with Shanghai RAAS, we are we're adapting to the evolving market environment by broadening our reach across Tier 2 hospitals and retail pharmacies, increasing our marketing and engagement with local and regional bodies and pushing our medical teams to expand albumin-related disease awareness. There is no silver bullet, but we are optimistic these efforts will deliver results over time.

In parallel, we are progressively developing opportunities beyond China to diversify our geographic exposure. The U.S. market is an important part of that effort where differentiated formats such as ALBUTEIN FlexBag can support our medium-term commercial development. We're also expanding our commercial focus into additional markets with attractive price structures and exploring cross-selling with other portfolio products where it creates value. Our priorities are clear: protect and strengthen our position in China through disciplined execution and the development of a more geographically diversified albumin franchise. Alpha-1 is a different type of opportunity. Here, value creation comes from developing a market where an estimated 80% to 90% of patients remain undiagnosed and as a result, untreated.

Our strategy to unlock this potential is built around three priorities: clinical evidence, treatment convenience and diagnosis. First, clinical evidence. SPARTA is designed to further strengthen the clinical evidence supporting augmentation therapy, evaluating both the current standard dose and a higher dose versus placebo. We continue to expect top line results in late Q4 '26 with a market presentation in Q1 '27, depending on timing. The outcome will be determined by the data, but positive results could help strengthen the evidence base and support broader awareness and access to treatment. Second, treatment convenience. Our Alpha-1 subcutaneous 15% program is now in Phase III, aimed at providing patients with greater flexibility and convenience in how they receive treatment. Third, diagnosis.

Clinical innovation alone will not unlock the full potential of this market. We also need to identify more patients. Alongside with our clinical programs, we are working to expand screening and improve diagnosis rate. One example is our partnership with AlphaDetect, aimed at accelerating patient identification and diagnosis. The earlier patients are diagnosed, the sooner they can access appropriate treatment. Together, these initiatives address three critical barriers to market development, strengthening clinical evidence, expanding treatment options and improving patient identification. As a global leader in Alpha-1, we have the expertise, commercial capabilities and clinical programs to help develop this market, and we are committed to capture the opportunities that will emerge.

Now I'd like to come back to Egypt, a central component of our value creation plan and where we are working in conjunction with the Egyptian government to support the country's goal of plasma self-sufficiency and improve access to plasma-derived medicines. Last year, we achieved full self-sufficiency in Factor VIII, albumin and Ig for Egypt, a notable milestone. Egypt is not simply about adding plasma collection capacity. It is about building an advantaged integrated source of plasma that will enable us to progressively optimize and improve our global sourcing footprint and cost profile.

Operationally, Egypt continues to scale with monthly plasma collection volumes nearly doubling since the beginning of the year, putting us on track to collect approximately 1 million liters in 2026. We continue to build out the integrated plasma ecosystem with 18 collection centers today expanding to 20 by the first quarter of 2027. And we expect to develop an additional 20 centers in the coming years to support 3 million liters of annual plasma collection in Egypt. In parallel, we continue to develop the fractionation, purification, testing and logistical infrastructure required to operate the platform end-to-end.

A critical milestone for Egypt has been the European Medical Authority regulatory approval, which enabled us to progressively integrate Egypt into our global plasma sourcing network to supply international markets. Integrating Egypt into our global network give us greater flexibility to optimize plasma allocation. As Egypt increasingly supplies international markets, we can make more efficient use of our U.S. collection infrastructure and retain U.S. collected plasma in the U.S. market where it creates the greatest value. Economics are equally important. Egypt has a structurally attractive plasma collection cost and higher protein yields, supporting margin expansion as volume scales.

This is the strategic opportunity Egypt represents a more competitive and flexible global plasma sourcing model with the potential to structurally improve our cost base and support meaningfully long-term value creation. That brings me back to the broader message of today's update. We are executing on our priorities, growing our core franchises, improving profitability and cash conversion, strengthening our balance sheet and advancing the strategic initiatives that will drive future value creation. And with that, let me hand it over to Rahul.

Rahul Srinivasan: Thank you, Nacho. Turning to Slide 12. Our financial highlights for Q3 and the first nine months of 2026. The key financial message from the first nine months is that the improvement in financial performance we anticipated in prior calls is materializing. Stronger operating performance is translating into higher profitability and cash generation, supporting continued deleveraging and greater financial flexibility. Before I begin, please note that the growth figures I discuss will be in constant currency, unless otherwise specified. Group net revenues reached EUR 2.04 billion in the quarter and EUR 5.614 billion through nine months, with Biopharma again leading the growth.

That operating momentum translated into adjusted EBITDA of EUR 538 million and continued improvement in group profit and free cash flow. Revenue growth accelerated to 8.4% in Q3, bringing growth through nine months to 4.6%, consistent with the second half improvement we anticipated. Reported gross margin reached 39.6% in Q3 and 38% through nine months, in line with the quarterly progression we anticipated. This improvement was achieved despite the year-to-date headwinds from the donor center network restructuring costs, Biotest ramping up Yimmugo sales, China albumin and the dissolution of the joint business in Diagnostics.

The main drivers of our gross margin expansion are volume growth and favorable product mix in Biopharma and further optimization of plasma sourcing and collection costs, including some initial small contributions from Egypt that will scale as our Egypt collections ramp up over time. Adjusted EBITDA reached EUR 538 million in the quarter and EUR 1.392 billion for the first nine months, representing 9.8% growth in the quarter and 5% growth year-to-date. Adjusted EBITDA margins for the quarter expanded 60 basis points to 26.4% and by 30 basis points to 24.8% for the nine-month period. For the full year, we continue to target an adjusted EBITDA margin of 25%, consistent with our guidance for the year.

Group profit through the first nine months increased 28.4% year-on-year to EUR 390 million, reflecting stronger operating performance and improved below-the-line expenses. We achieved EUR 298 million in free cash flow before M&A for the first nine months of 2026, up 59% or EUR 110 million year-on-year. We continue to be encouraged by our improvement in free cash flow performance, which I will elaborate upon in a few slides. These results demonstrate the operating leverage we are working to sustain over the medium term. Total net leverage stood at 3.98x and secured net leverage at 2.5x. Regulatory restrictions in China continue to affect the market and channel inventories remain elevated. Although we are seeing some early signs of improvement in sell-out, sell-in volumes remain under pressure. Destocking will take time, but China remains a critically important market for Grifols and the broader plasma industry. Taking a step back in 2026, we have constrained our IG volumes growth to deliver EBITDA growth and to better balance our last liter economics. In Alpha-1 and our Specialty Proteins portfolio, we had a very strong quarter. For Alpha-1, we are seeing higher treatment numbers as patient access conditions improve following a challenging reauthorization period early in the year. In June, our U.S. team launched FESILTY, our new fibrinogen concentrate for patients with congenital fibrinogen deficiency in the U.S., adding to our Specialty Proteins .

I also want to flag that given the phasing-related gains that have benefited our Q3 Biopharma results, please expect more modest Biopharma growth in Q4 that is lapping a strong sales quarter from Q4 2025. The 7% decline continues to reflect the dissolution of the QuidelOrtho joint business, an impact that will continue through the end of 2026. Excluding this effect, Diagnostics grew 2.3% on an underlying basis through nine months. The Diagnostics division remains focused on executing its multiyear repositioning plan.

We are pleased with the improvement in adjusted EBITDA in Q3 and nine months year-to-date. Even as we experienced more weakness than anticipated in albumin, continued volume growth and positive mix in IG, strong performance in our Alpha-1 and Specialty portfolio, optimization in our plasma cost per liter and good operating cost control drove 9.8% growth in adjusted EBITDA in Q3 and 5% growth through nine months.

Margins expanded by 60 basis points in Q3 and 30 basis points through nine months. For the year, we continue to target 25% adjusted EBITDA margin for the group. Over time, we expect our adjusted EBITDA to converge more with our reported EBITDA. These optimizations were unlocked by the EMA approval of Egyptian plasma and are positive for our long-term network efficiency. By shifting part of our resourcing to a more cost-effective EMA approved hub in Egypt, we are structurally derisking our plasma supply, expanding margins and reinforcing the underlying fundamentals of our business model.

Consistent with prior years, we will continue to assess the carrying value of certain noncore capitalized R&D projects as we apply greater discipline to capital allocation. None of these noncore projects impact the go-forward equity or credit story for Grifols. We expect to complete that assessment in Q4. Any resulting potential impairment would be noncash and would not affect adjusted EBITDA, free cash flow or credit agreement net leverage. Turning to Slide 15. I wanted to share more information about the moving pieces of our adjusted EBITDA margin progression this year. In Q3, we recovered to 30 basis points ahead of the prior year levels. This improvement was achieved despite incremental margin headwinds from Biotest Yimmugo sales, a Q3 accrual related to our Canadian plasma centers and continued China albumin weakness. The drivers behind the underlying improvement are Biopharma volume and price/mix, improving plasma costs and the early contributions from Egypt, all positive trends that we will work to continue in the coming years ahead. On the right-hand side, we show the operating expense evolution.

The story here is one of good cost containment while continuing to resource the business where it creates value. We expect to continue to apply this discipline to the business over the long term. Turning to Slide 16. We continue to deliver meaningful improvement in free cash flow and cash conversion, and we remain on track to deliver on our full year guidance for free cash flow pre- M&A. In the first nine months, free cash flow pre-M&A was EUR 298 million, or EUR 110 million better than 2025. As a percentage of EBITDA, free cash flow conversion through nine months improved meaningfully to more than 20%, albeit benefiting from some meaningful phasing-related gains.

The particular callouts on year-to-date free cash flow are on inventory, where we continue to invest to support the needs of our Biopharma business and CapEx taken together with capitalized IT and R&D spend as a percentage of sales continues to normalize from the 2024-2025 peak. Consistent with prior guidance, we expect cash interest costs to be in line with 2025 despite needing to refinance maturing attractively priced debt earlier this year and the Fed and ECB interest rate rises this year. And finally, please remember that the impact of euro-dollar FX movement is broadly neutral on free cash flow pre-M&A. In conclusion, our free cash flow trajectory is progressing as planned. Finally, Slide 17.

This slide runs through our leverage position and liquidity profile. We've made solid progress on the balance sheet, deleveraging entirely organically from 5.5x in June 2024. You will notice that this slide shows our most recent credit agreement net leverage position to two decimal places. I do that just to make the point that our credit agreement leverage is now finally below 4x. And I want to take the opportunity to recognize the efforts of the entire company and the Board. This has taken many years of hard work and discipline to achieve this important milestone. Of course, there remains further work to be done as we prioritize continued deleveraging alongside our other capital allocation objectives.

Alongside the strong organic deleveraging progress, we have significantly reshaped our liquidity profile in the last two years that currently stands at EUR 2.14 billion, over 3x the liquidity we had in September '24. This liquidity position gives us ample room to support our capital allocation objectives and manage our normal working capital needs. It additionally serves as a buffer to cover unexpected funding needs.

Most of this liquidity is from our undrawn revolving credit facility that does not have much of a cash interest drag, allowing us to run the business with optimized cash levels using any surplus cash to pay down debt, as we did with the redemption of EUR 500 million of our most expensive debt earlier this year. As you are aware, we do not have any significant maturities until the fourth quarter of 2028. And now most of the debt in our capital structure is either callable or prepayable without significant penalties, allowing us to be more opportunistic as we consider our refinancing or debt redemption strategies.

Looking forward, leverage should continue to progressively improve over time as adjusted EBITDA continues to grow and our improving free cash flow generation provides optionality to reduce debt over time. Given our year-to-date performance and our financial position, the Board has approved an interim dividend of EUR 0.15 per share payable in early December 2026. With that, let me hand it back to Nacho to conclude the presentation.

Jose Ignacio Abia Buenache: Let me take on SPARTA, Charles. And there is not much we can say. I think that the we plan to present the results in the Q1 of 2027. That's what is being tested, right? So with the primary endpoint to change from baseline in whole PD15 on CT densitometry measuring lung tissue density loss over time. So it's not a pharmacokinetic only study. So that's what we can say. Obviously, we don't have any idea about the results so far. But I think it's coming closer.

And as we say, as soon as we have the results at the end of this year, we will make the presentation of them in Q1 2027.

Rahul Srinivasan: And on IPO, Charles, look, it's a critical decision for the Board. They're being diligent in their assessment. My expectation is I do not expect an update on the IPO until 2027. Daniel Segarra: Thank you, Rahul. The next question is coming from Jaime. I guess that there is some follow-ups here. Jaime, please.

Jaime Escribano: Just a couple of follow-ups. So just to complete the top line outlook, if you can elaborate a little bit further on the Alpha-1 and especially, obviously, double-digit growth in Q3. Rahul Srinivasan: Sure, Jaime. Look, I think we guided on Alpha-1 and our Specialty Proteins . We guided to 5% mid-single-digit growth for the full year in '26. I will reiterate that. And in fact, in the annex, you will probably -- yes, you will see reference to an adjusted metric as well. But when you look at gross margin reported year-to-date versus '25, these were the key drivers.

China albumin was a headwind. Plasma center reorganization, a headwind. We talked about the diagnostic joint business as well being a small headwind. Then finally, Biotest, Yimmugo U.S. sales, which is very additive from a top line perspective, but in the short term, dilutive from a gross margin standpoint. So a lot happening in that gross margin reported number that needs to be unpicked. But if you look at the annex, you'll see the reference to some of the adjustments. But for me, as you stated as well at the -- in our Q4 call when we provided guidance for this year, I mentioned 38% as being the benchmark for the full year '26.

As you rightly say, we're already at that 38% level. and we go into our Q4 needing to replicate that 38% to achieve the full year number. So on track so far, so good, a bit of work to do in Q4 as well.

Daniel Segarra: Let's move to the next one. It comes from Guilherme, BPI.

Guilherme Sampaio: Yes. So again, on IG on the second half of the year. So you mentioned just a quarter ago that you might grow in the second half by mid- to high single digits. Possibly the low end of this target is quite conservative regarding Q4. But is the high end a good reference for the second half of the year? Rahul Srinivasan: Yes. So Egypt ramp-up, Egypt ramp-up, year-to-date Egypt ramp-up is very small in our gross margin numbers. Jose Ignacio Abia Buenache: And just to add on that, Guilherme, I think that our progress in Egypt is steady and continues. So we know that in this industry, and this is included in our indication, in the indication of all the products and all the IGs in the market, there is a potential number of adverse events. that obviously we work to minimize, but sometimes happen. It's, I would say, normal, but not infrequent that the regulatory authorities wants to take a look on that. This is not focused on Grifols by any mean. It's across the entire industry.

And as I say, it's nothing that has never happened. It happened from time to time. We take those obviously very seriously, and we work with the authorities on this. #3254. New Zealand’s central bank registers Revolut as the country’s 27th bank

The fintech has operated in the country since 2023 and plans savings and credit products, months after launching in Australia.

Revolut has been registered as a bank in New Zealand, clearing the way for the fintech to expand its financial services in the country.

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand announced the approval on Tuesday, local time, making Revolut Bank New Zealand the country’s 27th registered bank.

The London-based company has operated in New Zealand since July 2023. When it applied for registration in late 2024, it said approval would make it the first global digital bank in the country. It plans to introduce interest-paying savings accounts and a broader range of credit products.

“The Reserve Bank recognises the value that credible new entrants can bring,” said Scott McKinnon, the central bank’s director of specialist supervision.

He added that new banks can make the financial system more competitive, resilient and inclusive. However, the registration process remains rigorous, with every applicant assessed against the same banking requirements.

Revolut NZ has been registered under New Zealand’s current banking legislation. The framework will be replaced by the Deposit Takers Act, which is due to come into force on 1 December 2028, the central bank said.

“Launching our New Zealand bank marks another significant step in our mission to build the world’s first truly global bank. Securing our seventh bank licence and our fifth this year alone is a testament to our business model and our team. We are confident our offering will bring true competition to the New Zealand banking sector,” said Nik Storonsky, Founder and CEO of Revolut

The approval adds to a series of banking licence wins for Revolut over the past year. In March, the company secured its full UK banking licence after a multi-year wait.

In July, Australia’s regulator granted it an unrestricted banking licence, its first in the Asia-Pacific region. Revolut said it planned to invest A$400m to challenge Australia’s Big Four banks.

New Zealand’s banking market is dominated by the same four Australian banking groups, giving Revolut another opportunity to compete with established lenders. Matt Baxby, the company’s chief executive for Australia and New Zealand, has described the country as prime ground for expansion.

When Revolut applied for registration, it said it had more than 50 million customers worldwide. Its New Zealand business had already processed over NZ$350m in transactions by late 2024.

The expansion comes as Revolut continues to build its international presence ahead of a possible public listing. The company was valued at $75bn in a share sale last year, making it Europe’s most valuable private tech company.

Half an hour after today’s closing bell, Apple will report its earnings for the fourth fiscal quarter of 2026, followed by a conference call where Apple CEO John Ternus and CFO Kevan Parekh will discuss the results.

This will be Ternus’s first earnings call since taking over from Tim Cook in September, and the conversation will likely center on how Apple navigated another quarter of memory shortages and rising component costs, as well as how it expects those challenges to affect its performance going into the holiday season.

During its previous earnings call, Apple projected revenue growth of between 9% and 11% year over year, despite significantly greater supply constraints affecting the iPhone, Mac, and iPad. If that forecast holds, quarterly revenue should come in between $111.69 billion and $113.74 billion.

The results will include just a few days of sales of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, which launched on September 18. Apple should have been a lot more transparent about its plans

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's no secret that the iPhone Duo has been pretty hard to get hold of, despite the fact prices start at $2,000. The consensus has been that limited supply is the main factor, but Mark Gurman at Bloomberg has revealed a few more factors that could explain why you're having to wait so long for your own iPhone Duo.

One of the biggest factors is that, according to Gurman, Apple actually rushed the iPhone Duo to market. He claims Apple originally intended to wait until November to launch, and even then the foldable would initially only be released in the U.S. and China. Other regions would have to wait until later this year, or more likely into 2027.

In other words, Apple wasn't really prepared to meet the demand, which explains why the company admitted it was "nothing short of extraordinary" to see so many people try to get hold of one.

On top of that, Apple apparently decided that it was going to prioritize brick-and-mortar Apple Stores over the online purchasing experience. This means roughly 80% of Apple's supply of iPhone Duos were set aside for walk-in purchases over that first weekend of sales. This explains why launch-day deliveries and pickups all sold out within minutes of iPhone Duo pre-orders going live.

Apparently stores only had 50 to 250 units each, depending on their size and location. Gurman also notes high storage options and blue units were in particularly short supply — and you'd likely need to camp out to get your hands on one.

Plus, as is the case with any high-profile product launch, scalpers have been using bots to monitor the Apple website and buy up as much stock as they can. That includes reserving any units that do become available for in-store pickup.

Considering scalpers have become a plague over the past several years, Apple should have seen that coming. It's possible that the emphasis on in-store sales was an attempt to try and curb the use of bots and prevent the minority of would-be scalpers from stockpiling Duo units.

Considering scalpers have become a plague over the past several years, Apple should have seen that coming.

But that obviously doesn't work if a) Apple doesn't tell anyone what's going on and b) scalpers are still able to reserve devices for in-store pickup en masse. The lack of transparency is definitely exacerbating the problems of getting hold of an iPhone Duo.

If you're looking to get an iPhone Duo, your only real option is to be patient and wait for Apple, carriers and major retailers to get one to you. It's possible that you may be able to snatch one up for in-store pickup if you're vigilant (and fast), but when you're competing with bots that task becomes significantly harder.

Obviously the last thing you want to do is buy a scalper unit for an inflated price. Not only are you wasting your money, you're encouraging this kind of behavior — and the more scalpers are emboldened, the more they'll do. Stuff costs enough right now without scalpers inserting themselves as middle men.

#3250. Why AI Can’t Replace Engineering Teams

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

How to convince your boss LLMs can’t do it all

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

If you’re an engineer, you may feel like your skills aren’t commanding the premium they once did. Many engineers have faced layoffs or restructuring. But even for those of us who still have jobs, something corrosive is happening. You may have heard some version of this:

“ChatGPT answered that in five seconds. Why can’t you?”

Or, “I made this app in a weekend. Why is our team taking so long?”

I worked on a team where leadership said things like this directly to engineers. This was in 2024 and 2025, when the AI craze was in full swing and Claude and ChatGPT adoption was rising.

Generative AI (and the marketing behind it) gives people the illusion that the work is simpler than it is. A working demo hides complexity, and once someone has a website that works, they may decide they no longer need engineers, or start to distrust the ones they do have.

Some CEOs want to believe they can replace an engineering team with a few sexy prompts. Many companies also want them to believe this.

That website works great in the demo—under specific conditions and without users with thumbs for fingers. Then it has to plug into a system with millions of lines of old code, satisfy legal requirements, meet accessibility standards, and be delivered in a complex deployment process.

Thinking that writing code was the only bottleneck for deploying new software is like the Titanic seeing the tip of the iceberg and assuming there was nothing underneath it.

Engineers have a unique position in the AI space, because you have the capacity to understand how these models work much better than the average person. Use this to your advantage.

Learn how AI models work. If you can’t already explain that LLMs are probabilistic, what tokens are, or why training data matters, spend a weekend fixing that. You don’t need to become a full-blown AI researcher. A few fundamentals will put you ahead of most people making the AI decisions.

Teach upward. Turn that knowledge into teaching moments for the people who lead you. Explain the limits of these tools, and why a demo and a production system are different animals. It keeps people from truly believing that a notebook full of prompts can replace an engineering team.

Consider the criticism of today’s processes. Some of what we do has been treated as ceremony for too long. Be willing to say, “you know what, maybe you’re right, this process is too slow for the speed we can work at now.” Conceding that earns you the credibility to defend the steps that matter.

I still believe that speed at the cost of everything else is harmful—but that’s a topic for another time.

Find your voice. Engineers at the forefront of AI adoption need to push back and explain why we do things the way we do. Nobody else in the room is going to do it for us.

Your goal, in my opinion, is to save your organization from buying into the hype so much that they chase the wrong thing. Our job, before and after AI, is building safe and useful products for human beings, and engineers are still best suited for that.

The need to educate engineering students about ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, but today’s curricula often miss the mark. Three professors propose a new approach: adding ethics training directly to core technical coursework.

Looking for a career in quantum computing hardware? An IBM spin-off called Anderon could receive up to $1 billion in funding from the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act for its quantum foundry, established earlier this year. Could Anderon do for quantum hardware what TSMC did for conventional chips?

When Gurmeet Saran joined Anthropic’s technical staff in 2025, he entered a role focused on a key question: How do you know whether you can trust a chatbot like Claude? Learn more about Saran’s path and his work at the AI company.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, an online education platform that helps people break into AI and modern software roles through project-based learning and one-on-one mentorship with senior developers. Parsity helps career changers transition into software by focusing on practical skills, real-world systems, and the kind of experience companies actually look for.Outside Parsity, Brian works a senior software engineer in the SF Bay Area.Brian is also a father of three, and when he’s not working with students or building programs, you might catch him running around Lake Merritt in Oakland, California.

What was wrong with the headline "Engineering Jobs That AI Can't Replace"?

#3249. Why Rivian Stock Popped Today

Rapidly rising R2 sales could pave the way for further gains for shareholders.

Shares of Rivian Automotive (RIVN +8.47%) rose more than 8% on Monday, following bullish analyst commentary.

The Rivian R2. Image source: Rivian Automotive.

Rivian's revenue jumped 38% year over year to nearly $2.2 billion in the third quarter. The electric vehicle (EV) maker's deliveries increased 46% to 19,248 vehicles, fueled by sales of its new midsize SUV, the Rivian R2.

"Customer and media feedback on R2 has been exceptional," CEO RJ Scaringe said in the company's Q3 earnings release.

Rivian, in turn, boosted its full-year delivery target to 67,000 to 70,000 vehicles, up from a prior forecast of 65,000 to 70,000.

UBS analyst Joseph Spak believes Rivian has more room to run. He sees the EV upstart's share price rising another 30% to $17.

Spak thinks investors should consider buying Rivian's stock ahead of a forthcoming ramp in R2 sales. He expects fast-growing sales volumes of the more affordable SUV to drive Rivian's margins higher, hastening its push toward profitability.

Rivian's adjusted net loss per share narrowed to $0.48 in the third quarter from $0.65 in the year-ago period.

Spak also highlighted Rivian's software and services segment as another potential profit driver. The division's third-quarter revenue and gross profit surged 45% and 66%, respectively, to $605 million and $256 million.

#3248. Apple spyware alerts reach German MPs and journalists in 99 countries

Germany’s government says it is taking the warnings very seriously. Apple’s latest spyware alerts reached users in 99 countries, including journalists in Turkey and Lebanon who have gone public.

Apple threat notification on the Lock Screen and in Settings.

Germany’s cybersecurity agency has told lawmakers who got Apple’s spyware warnings to treat their iPhones as possibly compromised. Several Bundestag members and other public figures have received the alerts since 29 October. The Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) said so in a note on its website.

In the alerts, Apple says it detected an attack using mercenary spyware. The BSI describes this as commercially built spyware that state actors have often used against specific people.

The agency said it does not know whether attackers broke into the phones or only tried to. It wrote to Bundestag members about the threat on 30 October and asked anyone affected to contact it directly.

“Those affected who have received a corresponding warning message from Apple should therefore assume that their device may have been compromised,” the BSI wrote (translated from German).

Government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius spoke to the Financial Times. He did not say which members of the federal government the attackers targeted.

The government is “taking the incident and the warning very seriously,” Kornelius told the FT.

Unless someone plans a forensic analysis, the BSI advises updating the phone’s software at once. It also recommends switching on Apple’s Lockdown Mode and keeping it on, even on a new device. Lockdown Mode makes new attacks harder, the agency said, but it does not remove an existing infection.

Anyone who judges the risk to be high should consider a new phone. They should also reset every account used on it and change their number. The BSI also listed a new passcode, new passwords, two-factor authentication and fresh PINs for Signal and WhatsApp.

Once inside a phone, this kind of spyware can read messages, including those in encrypted apps, the BSI said. It can also switch on the camera and microphone. In known cases it arrived through “zero-click” attacks that need no action from the victim. In October, Citizen Lab reported that an Israeli ad firm had used online ads to spread Candiru spyware.

Apple has sent these alerts several times a year since 2021. They have reached users in more than 150 countries, according to its support page. It calls them high-confidence warnings, but it does not name attackers or regions.

Threat researcher Costin Raiu flagged the new round on X on 30 October. He wrote that it was separate from Apple’s August wave and tied to new attacks. The notice he shared says this round went to targeted users in 99 countries.

Raiu told Suzanne Smalley of The Record that he had checked several victims’ notifications.

“So far we do not see any signs of compromise in the logs that could confirm which actor is responsible for the breaches,” Raiu told The Record.

Ragıp Soylu, Turkey bureau chief for Middle East Eye, posted his alert on X on Thursday. He called it a “badge of honour” and his third this year.

“Likely state actors using mercenary spyware have repeatedly tried to hack my phone,” Soylu wrote.

Radwan Mortada, a Lebanese investigative journalist and documentary filmmaker, wrote on X on 30 October that he had received the warning the day before. He said NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware had targeted him in 2017 and 2021.

His alert came days after the release of The Trap, his Al Jazeera 360 film about the September 2024 pager explosions in Lebanon. Israel has confirmed it carried out those attacks against Hezbollah members. After the film came out, Mortada told The Record, Israeli soldiers entered his family home in southern Lebanon, looted it and blew it up.

He said he has no concrete evidence of a link to the spyware alert.

“The sequence of events, and their timing in relation to my investigative work, raise serious questions that cannot simply be dismissed,” Mortada told The Record.

“Targeting journalists with spyware poses a serious threat to freedom of the press and the confidentiality of their sources,” Mortada wrote on X (translated from Arabic).

John Scott-Railton, a researcher at Citizen Lab, told The Record that Apple made its alerts more visible in August.

“Apple Threat Notifications make accountability happen,” Scott-Railton said.

Germany’s federal police have bought Pegasus themselves. In 2021, the government told the Bundestag’s interior committee that the federal police office, the BKA, had bought a version of it, DW reported.

Spyware has reached European politicians before. In July, an EU lawmaker who investigated spyware abuse said attackers had hacked him with Pegasus. In Greece, victims of the Predator spyware are suing its maker for €8m.

My backyard is looking spectacular with the autumnal tones of gold and russet leaves. And I don’t even mind as they drift onto my lawn, creating a beautiful carpet of color.

But while I’m happy for them to settle for a short while, I won’t leave them all through winter, because although I appreciate their current aesthetic, over time they’ll damage my lawn.

A light flurry of leaves is not so much of a problem, but once your lawn gets covered in a carpet of fallen leaves, it can harm its health if they are not removed.

A thick layer of leaves is an open invitation to fungal disease, as the decaying matter traps moisture, blocks airflow and starves the grass of sunlight. This dark and damp microclimate is the perfect environment for fungi to thrive.

The layer of fallen leaves acts like a blanket, holding in rain, dew and condensation. And once the leaves are left there for a prolonged period, snow mold, brown patch and leaf blight will develop.

If your lawn is lightly covered with leaves, you can leave them be. The wind may help disperse some, while the rest will decompose and add nutrients to the soil.

However, if your lawn is covered in a deep pile of leaves, there’s little chance of sunlight reaching the blades of grass, and the trapped moisture won't dry out. In this scenario, you need to grab a rake and remove the leaves to prevent disease from becoming rife. If you don’t fancy the workout that raking leaves provides or you want to save time, you could also opt for a leaf blower or lawn sweeper.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Besides being a magnet for fungal disease, if leaves are left on your lawn, they can also attract pests. The leaf canopy can provide cover, warmth, moisture, and, once the leaves break down, food.

This metal rake comes with an adjustable head that can expand from 7-23 inches to suit your task. This allows it to pick up large leaves, clippings and lawn debris with ease, and it's also small enough to fit under hedges.

Whether you choose to rake or mow over your leaves, always aim for dry conditions. But if the forecast doesn’t look promising, clear what you can anyway — leaving a layer of wet leaves will suffocate your lawn and invite disease.

If the leaf cover is light, rather than a thick carpet, mowing is the faster route. Just ensure the leaves aren’t soaked to avoid clogging your mower. Best of all, mowing your leaves turns them into a valuable organic mulch, putting the goodness back into your soil.

#3245. From Chip Lab to Center Stage

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

This integrated circuit designer explains wearables to consumers

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

IEEE Member Preethi Ashwath is one of the few women who work in analog integrated circuit design, where about 11 percent are female.

Many engineers are more comfortable working behind the scenes developing technology than speaking to consumers about products. But Preethi Ashwath has learned to take center stage, talking about the “hearable” and wearable devices she has had a hand in developing as an analog integrated circuit designer in the consumer electronics division at Analog Devices of Wilmington, Mass.

The IEEE member is one of the few women who work in the specialized field, where about 11 percent are female, according to career platform Zippia.

Preethi Ashwath Employer Analog Devices, in BostonTitle Integrated circuit designerMember grade MemberAlma maters SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

Ashwath stepped out from behind the scenes last year to meet with attendees at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. She demonstrated Analog’s new earbuds, which track people’s heart and lung health through vibrations in their ear canals.

After she demonstrated her ability to explain the technology to consumers in simple terms, Analog selected her to represent the company at other events. She says she has “come to see speaking as part of contributing to the field, rather than something separate from technical work.”

She also gives technical talks on various aspects of electrostatic discharge (ESD) and other topics, as well as participates in panel discussions, she says, because they “reach engineers well beyond my immediate team.”

Ashwath is an active volunteer with the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society.

“Whether through designing semiconductor products, publishing technical articles, reviewing conference papers, or speaking at industry events, I try to contribute to the growth of the engineering community and the advancement of the field,” she says.

Ashwath, who grew up in Bengaluru, India, learned about electronics engineering from her high school physics tutor.

That introduction led her to take electronics as one of her core courses in her final years there. At the time, Ashwath’s older sister was pursuing an engineering degree.

“Between my interest in electronics and seeing her already on that path, it became clear to me that engineering was the way to go,” Ashwath says.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in electronics and communications engineering at the SJB Institute of Technology, in Bengaluru, she wanted to pursue a career in very-large-scale integration. But that changed once she moved to the United States and began her master’s program in electrical engineering at the University of California, Irvine.

She discovered her passion for circuits and devices during an internship at Intel in Santa Clara, Calif. She learned about circuit design, package design, and reliability verification tools such as Ansys Totem.

“Seeing every layer of the chip development process gave me a more complete picture of what goes into building a semiconductor product,” she says. “Through that experience, I realized I felt most connected to design.

“It was the hard work and creativity that drew me in. You start with a specification, build a circuit, simulate it, then wait for the chip to come back from fabrication. When your design works, it’s a real feeling of satisfaction. It teaches you patience and perseverance.”

After attaining her master’s degree, she was hired by Intel as an analog design engineer. She gained experience in mixed-signal circuit design before joining Analog. In her current role, she works on consumer hearables such as earbuds and wearables including fitness trackers and health monitors.

Her main focus is designing ESD pad rings, the borders of specialized circuits built around a microchip’s outermost edge to protect it from the discharge, which can damage circuit paths or introduce latent defects that lead to failures later in the chip’s life cycle.

“On a chip with multiple voltage domains, you have to plan how the protection structures are placed and connected across the whole pad ring—and get it right,” Ashwath says. “A mistake there could cause a chip to fail in the field in ways that are very hard to debug afterward.

“It’s detailed work that requires understanding both the device physics and how the whole chip fits together.”

Part of the job is designing and creating an integrated circuit’s building blocks, including ESD protection structures and other mixed-signal blocks. Ashwath conducts rigorous checks to verify they work as intended before being integrated into a chip.

She collaborates with ESD advisors, layout designers, and the digital team that designs the chip’s digital logic.

“I work with them to make sure my analog circuits and their digital blocks work together correctly,” she says. “No two days look exactly the same.”

In 2024 she was recognized with the company’s Impact Award for her “exceptional work on a critical project with significant cross-functional business impact.”

Ashwath was selected to represent Analog at events after a senior leader encouraged her to ask for high-visibility opportunities, she says.

“Most of my time is spent on designing circuits and simulations,” she says. “At CES, I stood in front of customers, engineers, and members of the press, explaining our technology and answering questions on the spot.”

The earbuds she demonstrated monitor minute vibrations from a user’s heart and lungs, according to the Analog website. The vibrations can detect arrhythmia, a leaky heart valve, or fluid in the lungs.

“Hearables are evolving from playing back audio to becoming health-monitoring platforms,” she says. “The ear turns out to be a good location for picking up physiological signals, so these devices can capture vital signs while someone is simply wearing them normally.

“The hard part is achieving high signal quality. The signals you’re trying to detect are very small and buried in the noise from the person’s movements and the surrounding environment.

“That’s where analog front-end design becomes critical. Extracting a meaningful signal from a noisy real-world environment is fundamentally an analog problem.”

Being face-to-face with customers at the conference was new to her.

“What struck me most was seeing how people react to the technology,” she says. “When you’re designing a block, you’re focused on specifications and margins. At CES, after explaining what the product does, I had a better understanding of why it matters to them.

“That connection between the circuit work and the final product is something you don’t always see from the design bench.”

Since the CES, Ashwath has presented other technologies she’s worked on. At the annual National Association of Music Merchants show in Anaheim, Calif., she demonstrated the A2B Automotive Audio Bus to the audio industry. The bus uses a low-cost unshielded twisted-pair cable to carry multichannel digital audio, control data, synchronized clock signals, and power in fewer than 50 microseconds, according to Analog.

“IEEE connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

At the company’s Global Technology Conference—an internal event held in Boston that draws engineers from the company’s more than 50 sites around the world—Ashwath led a demonstration of its solutions for augmented reality smart glasses.

“Each of these events has a different audience,” she says. “Learning to explain my technical work to different people has become a skill I’ve acquired.”

The most rewarding part of her job, she says, is seeing the end result of her work.

“You spend months on a design, and there’s a long wait between finishing it and finding out whether your instincts were right,” she says. “When the measurements match what you simulated, that’s the most satisfying moment in this job.

“The other part is knowing my work ends up in a real product. The circuits I design go into devices people actually use every day.”

Like many engineers, Ashwath joined IEEE to access research published in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. It keeps her current in a field that keeps moving, she says.

During her first year of membership, in 2021, she discovered other perks including networking and educational opportunities.

“IEEE connects you to a community outside your own company,” she says. “Attending lectures and technical talks exposes you to approaches and problems you wouldn’t encounter in your own work.”

She eventually began seeking out volunteer opportunities, specifically with IEEE conferences and journals, because they are “how you stay current with what’s happening in circuits and systems beyond your own day-to-day work,” she says.

“As an analog designer,” she says, “being connected to that broader community matters. The field moves, and you need a way to keep learning from it.”

She serves as a peer reviewer of papers for several IEEE conferences including the IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems and the IEEE International Midwest Symposium on Circuits and Systems. ISCAS is the flagship conference of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society. MWSCAS is the oldest U.S. conference on the technologies.

“Someone has to assess whether submitted work is technically sound and worth presenting,” she says, “and that only happens if practicing engineers are willing to put in the time.”

The combination of learning from the community and contributing to it is what makes her membership worthwhile, she says.

“Analog design is a field where you’re always learning. Just when you feel you understand one architecture, there’s another one to learn,” she says. “Being an active learner isn’t optional in this field; it’s the requirement, and being part of the IEEE community helps with that.

“IEEE also connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry.

“Reviewing papers means reading what researchers are working on, which is often quite different from how the same problems get approached in a product environment. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3243. MagSafe Monday: Pelican’s MagSafe Battery Pack is the battery built to go anywhere

A few weeks ago, I wrote about why the Pelican MagSafe Wallet is my favorite wallet for the fall, and the short version was that it’s built for being out and about. The Pelican MagSafe Battery Pack is the exact same idea applied to a power bank: a 5,000mAh MagSafe battery wrapped in a hardshell that’s meant to tossed around,

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Most MagSafe batteries are built for knowledge worker travel. Smooth plastic, a glossy finishe, and a body that picks up scratches the first time it shares a pocket with your keys, AirPods, etc. Pelican has been making cases for cameras and gear that survive the back of a truck for a long time, and their MagSafe pack carries that over. The hardshell exterior is designed to handle bumps and scratches, and the battery inside is protected rather than the thing doing the protecting.

For hiking, a day at the park, a camping trip, or a weekend of yard work with an audiobook going, this is the right trade-off.

The Pelican MagSafe Battery Pack is 5,000mAh, which is about one full charge for a standard iPhone and a solid top-up for a Pro Max. It charges via MagSafe at up to 15 watts, and the magnets are strong enough to stay put while the phone is in a jacket pocket or clipped to a backpack strap. It also works with any Qi device, so AirPods or a Samsung phone with a magnetic case will charge on it.

There’s a USB-C port for anything without MagSafe, with USB output and a short cable in the box. Four LEDs on the side show its remaining charge, which is still the simplest way to know whether to grab the battery or the wall charger before you walk out the door.

Two things to know going in. This is a 15-watt battery, not a Qi2.2 25-watt model, so it won’t match the fast-charging speeds you’ll see on the newer MagSafe batteries. For an outdoor MagSafe battery that spends most of its time topping up an iPhone in a pocket, I don’t think that matters much. The bigger one is the recharge speed.
